old: The acquisition of wealth is like the gathering together of an assembly for a theatre; its expenditure is like the breaking up of that assembly
modern: Wealth gathers like a crowd coming to watch a play, and it disappears like the crowd leaving when the play ends.

old: Wealth is perishable; let those who obtain it immediately practise those (virtues) which are imperishable
modern: Wealth is fleeting, so as soon as you acquire it, you should use it to do enduring good deeds.

old: Time, which shows itself (to the ignorant) as if it were something (real) is in the estimation of the wise (only) a saw which cuts down life
modern: Time looks to the ignorant like something real, but to the wise it is only a saw cutting through life.

old: Let virtuous deeds be done quickly, before the hiccup comes making the tongue silent
modern: Do good deeds quickly before you lose control of your tongue and your breathing becomes heavy and gurgling.

old: This world possesses the greatness that one who yesterday was is not today
modern: This world has the greatness of being able to say that someone who existed yesterday is not today.

old: Innumerable are the thoughts which occupy the mind of (the unwise), who know not that they shall live another moment
modern: Someone who does not know if they will live another moment will think of countless things.

old: The love of the soul to the body is like (the love of) a bird to its egg which it flies away from and leaves empty
modern: The soul's friendship with the body is like a bird leaving its egg and flying away.

old: Death is like sleep; birth is like awaking from it
modern: Death is like sleep, and birth is like waking from it.

old: It seems as if the soul, which takes a temporary shelter in a body, had not attained a home
modern: The life that takes temporary shelter in a body seems never to have found a home.

old: Whatever thing, a man has renounced, by that thing; he cannot suffer pain
modern: A person does not suffer pain from whatever thing they have detached themselves from.

old: After a man has renounced (all things), there will still be many things in this world (which he may enjoy); if he should desire them, let him, while it is time abandon (the world)
modern: Even after renouncing, many things remain in this world that may be desired, so give them up while there is still time.

old: Let the five senses be destroyed; and at the same time, let everything be abandoned that (the ascetic) has (formerly) desired
modern: One must control the five senses and their desires, and at the same time, let go of everything one has desired.

old: To be altogether destitute is the proper condition of those who perform austerities; if they possess anything, it will change (their resolution) and bring them back to their confused state
modern: Owning nothing at all is the proper condition of those who practise austerity, because owning anything will change their resolve and bring them back to confusion.

old: What means the addition of other things those who are attempting to cut off (future) births, when even their body is too much (for them)
modern: Even the physical body is a heavy burden for those trying to cut off future births, so why should they add even more attachments?

old: He who destroys the pride which says "I", "mine" will enter a world which is difficult even to the Gods to attain.
modern: Someone who destroys the pride that says "I" and "mine" will enter a world that even the gods find hard to reach.

old: Sorrows will never let go their hold of those who give not up their hold of desire
modern: Those who do not let go of their attachments will never be let go by grief.

old: Those who have entirely renounced (all things and all desire) have obtained (absorption into God); all others wander in confusion, entangled in the net of (many) births
modern: Those who have completely renounced everything attain the highest state, while those who do not renounce are deluded and trapped in the net of birth.

old: At the moment in which desire has been abandoned, (other) births will be cut off; when that has not been done, instability will be seen
modern: The moment desire is given up, further births are cut off; while it is not given up, everything remains unstable.

old: Desire the desire of Him who is without desire; in order to renounce desire, desire that desire
modern: Bind yourself to the one who is without attachments, and by doing so, you will break all your other attachments.

old: Inglorious births are produced by the confusion (of mind) which considers those things to be real which are not real
modern: Inglorious births come from the confused mind that takes what is unreal to be real.

old: A clear, undimmed vision of things will deliver its possessors from the darkness of future births, and confer the felicity (of heaven)
modern: A clear, undimmed view of things frees those who have it from the darkness of future births and gives them lasting happiness.

old: Heaven is nearer than earth to those men of purified minds who are freed from from doubt
modern: For people of purified mind who are free from doubt, heaven is nearer than earth.

old: Even those who have all the knowledge which can be attained by the five senses, will derive no benefit from it, if they are without a knowledge of the true nature of things
modern: Even if someone has fully mastered their five senses and their mind, it is useless to them if they do not know the true nature of reality.

old: (True) knowledge is the perception concerning every thing of whatever kind, that that thing is the true thing
modern: True knowledge is seeing the real nature of a thing, regardless of how it appears.

old: They, who in this birth have learned to know the True Being, enter the road which returns not into this world
modern: Those who learn and realize the true nature of reality in this lifetime will attain the path of no return, meaning they will not be born into this world again.

old: Let it not be thought that there is another birth for him whose mind having thoroughly considered (all it has been taught) has known the True Being
modern: Do not think there is another birth for someone whose mind has thoroughly considered what it learned and known the true reality.

old: True knowledge consists in the removal of ignorance; which is (the cause of) births, and the perception of the True Being who is (the bestower of) heaven
modern: True knowledge is removing the ignorance that causes births and perceiving the true reality that grants heaven.

old: He who so lives as to know Him who is the support of all things and abandon all desire, will be freed from the evils which would otherwise cleave to him and destroy (his efforts after absorption)
modern: If someone understands the ultimate reality and lives without attachment, the suffering that once clung to them will be destroyed and will not return.

old: If the very names of these three things, desire, anger, and confusion of mind, be destroyed, then will also perish evils (which flow from them)
modern: If the very names of desire, anger, and delusion are destroyed, then the diseases and sorrows they cause will also disappear.

old: (The wise) say that the seed, which produces unceasing births, at all times, to all creatures, is desire
modern: Desire is the seed that causes endless birth for all living things at all times.

old: If anything be desired, freedom from births should be desired; that (freedom from births) will be attained by desiring to be without desire
modern: If you must desire anything, desire freedom from birth, and that is reached by desiring to be without desire.

old: There is in this world no excellence equal to freedom from desire; and even in that world, there is nothing like it
modern: There is no wealth in this world or any other that is equal to the wealth of not wanting anything.

old: Purity (of mind) consists in freedom from desire; and that (freedom from desire) is the fruit of the love of truth
modern: Purity of mind is freedom from desire, and that freedom is the fruit of loving truth.

old: They are said to be free (from future birth) who are freed from desire; all others (who, whatever else they may be free from, are not freed from desire) are not thus free
modern: Those who are free from desire are truly free, while others are not free even if they are free from other things.

old: It is the chief duty of (an ascetic) to watch against desire with (jealous) fear; for it has power to deceive (and destroy) him
modern: Desire is what deceives and destroys a person, so living with fear of desire is virtue.

old: If a man thoroughly cut off all desire, the deeds, which confer immortality, will come to him, in the path in which he seeks them
modern: If a person completely eliminates desire, they will achieve immortal deeds in the path they choose.

old: There is no sorrow to those who are without desire; but where that is, (sorrow) will incessantly come, more and more
modern: There is no sorrow for those without desire, but where desire exists, sorrow comes endlessly and without end.

old: Even while in this body, joy will never depart (from the mind, in which) desire, that sorrow of sorrows, has been destroyed
modern: If the greatest sorrow, which is desire, is destroyed, then joy will never cease.

old: The removal of desire, whose nature it is never to be satisfied, will immediately confer a nature that can never be changed
modern: If someone gets rid of an insatiable desire that is never fulfilled, that very state will give them a permanent, unchanging blissful nature.

old: Perseverance comes from a prosperous fate, and idleness from an adverse fate
modern: When fate brings wealth, effort follows; when fate brings loss, laziness follows.

old: An adverse fate produces folly, and a prosperous fate produces enlarged knowledge
modern: A fate that causes loss makes a person foolish, while a fate that brings gain expands their knowledge.

old: Although (a man) may study the most polished treatises, the knowledge which fate has decreed to him will still prevail
modern: Even if someone studies many subtle texts, their innate wisdom will still prevail.

old: There are (through fate) two different natures in the world, hence the difference (observable in men) in (their acquisition of) wealth, and in their attainment of knowledge
modern: Through fate, the world has two different natures, which is why some people gain wealth while others attain wisdom.

old: In the acquisition of property, every thing favourable becomes unfavourable, and (on the other hand) everything unfavourable becomes favourable, (through the power of fate)
modern: When trying to make wealth, fate causes good things to turn bad and bad things to turn good.

old: Whatever is not conferred by fate cannot be preserved although it be guarded with most painful care; and that, which fate has made his, cannot be lost, although one should even take it and throw it away
modern: Things not meant for you will not stay with you no matter how carefully you guard them, and things that are meant for you will not leave you even if you throw them away.

old: Even those who gather together millions will only enjoy them, as it has been determined by the disposer (of all things)
modern: Even those who gather millions can only enjoy them according to what has been determined by the disposer of all things.

old: The destitute will renounce desire (and become ascetics), if (fate) do not make them suffer the hindrances to which they are liable, and they pass away
modern: If the poor are spared from the suffering that fate usually brings them, they will give up their desires and become ascetics.

old: How is it that those, who are pleased with good fortune, trouble themselves when evil comes, (since both are equally the decree of fate) ?
modern: People who are happy when good things happen should not be sad when bad things happen, since both are just part of life.

old: What is stronger than fate ? If we think of an expedient (to avert it), it will itself be with us before (the thought)
modern: What is stronger than fate? Whenever we think of a way to avoid it, it is already there ahead of the thought.

old: He who possesses these six things, an army, a people, wealth, ministers, friends and a fortress, is a lion among kings
modern: A king who possesses an army, a loyal population, wealth, a minister, allies, and a fort is a lion among kings.

old: Never to fail in these four things, fearlessness, liberality, wisdom, and energy, is the kingly character
modern: A king should never lack courage, generosity, wisdom, and energy.

old: These three things, viz, vigilance, learning, and bravery, should never be wanting in the ruler of a country
modern: A ruler of a country should never lack these three: alertness, learning, and bravery.

old: He is a king who, with manly modesty, swerves not from virtue, and refrains from vice
modern: A king who never strays from virtue and never commits vice, and who is never without courage and honor, is the best ruler.

old: He is a king who is able to acquire (wealth), to lay it up, to guard, and to distribute it
modern: A capable king is someone who creates ways to earn wealth, accumulates it, protects it from being stolen by others, and spends it on righteousness, prosperity, and happiness.

old: The whole world will exalt the country of the king who is easy of access, and who is free from harsh language
modern: The whole world will exalt the country of a ruler who is easy to approach and free from harsh speech.

old: The world will praise and submit itself to the mind of the king who is able to give with affability, and to protect all who come to him
modern: The world will praise and submit to the ruler who can give with kindness and protect everyone who comes to them.

old: That king, will be esteemed a God among men, who performs his own duties, and protects (his subjects).
modern: A king who performs his duties properly and protects his people will be considered a god by them.

old: The whole world will dwell under the umbrella of the king, who can bear words that embitter the ear
modern: A king who can endure harsh words will have the whole world living under his protection.

old: He is the light of kings who has there four things, beneficence, benevolence, rectitude, and care for his people
modern: A king who has generosity, grace, just rule, and care for the weak is a guiding light for all other kings.

old: Let a man learn thoroughly whatever he may learn, and let his conduct be worthy of his learning
modern: Learn whatever you study without any mistakes, and then live your life in a way that is worthy of what you have learned.

old: Letters and numbers are the two eyes of man
modern: Letters and numbers are the two eyes of all living beings.

old: The learned are said to have eyes, but the unlearned have (merely) two sores in their face
modern: The learned are said to have eyes, while the ignorant have two sores on their face.

old: It is the part of the learned to give joy to those whom they meet, and on leaving, to make them think (Oh! when shall we meet them again.)
modern: It is the mark of the learned that meeting them gives joy and leaving them makes people wonder when they will meet again.

old: The unlearned are inferior to the learned, before whom they stand begging, as the destitute before the wealthy
modern: The unlearned stand before the learned as the destitute stand begging before the wealthy.

old: Water will flow from a well in the sand in proportion to the depth to which it is dug, and knowledge will flow from a man in proportion to his learning
modern: The deeper you dig a sandy well, the more water flows out, and similarly, the more a person learns, the more knowledge they gain.

old: How is it that any one can remain without learning, even to his death, when (to the learned man) every country is his own (country), and every town his own (town) ?
modern: A learned person can treat any country as their own and any town as their home, so why does someone spend their life until death without learning anything?

old: The learning, which a man has acquired in one birth, will yield him pleasure during seven births
modern: The knowledge a person learns in a single lifetime will help them for seven lifetimes.

old: The learned will long (for more learning), when they see that while it gives pleasure to themselves, the world also derives pleasure from it
modern: Learned people will want to learn more when they see that their knowledge brings pleasure to both themselves and the world.

old: Learning is the true imperishable riches; all other things are not riches
modern: Learning is the best wealth that cannot be destroyed; nothing else is true wealth.

old: To speak in an assembly (of the learned) without fullness of knowledge, is like playing at chess (on a board) without squares
modern: Speaking in a gathering without having studied the books that give full knowledge is like playing checkers without drawing a board.

old: The desire of the unlearned to speak (in an assembly), is like a woman without breasts desiring (the enjoyment of ) woman-hood
modern: An uneducated person wanting to speak in an assembly is like a woman without breasts desiring womanhood.

old: The unlearned also are very excellent men, if they know how to keep silence before the learned
modern: Someone who is uneducated is considered a very good person if they remain silent in the presence of the learned.

old: Although the natural knowledge of an unlearned man may be very good, the wise will not accept for true knowledge
modern: Even if an uneducated person has excellent natural knowledge, a wise person will not accept it as true knowledge.

old: The self-conceit of an unlearned man will fade away, as soon as he speaks in an assembly (of
modern: An unlearned person's pride disappears when they speak in front of knowledgeable people.

old: The unlearned are like worthless barren land: all that can be said of them is, that they exist
modern: Unlearned people are said to exist, but they are like barren land that yields nothing because they are of no use to themselves or to others.

old: The beauty and goodness of one who is destitute of knowledge by the study of great and exquisite works, is like (the beauty and goodness) of a painted earthen doll
modern: The beauty and goodness of someone who has not studied great and subtle works is like that of a painted clay doll.

old: Wealth, gained by the unlearned, will give more sorrow than the poverty which may come upon the learned
modern: Wealth in the hands of the unlearned causes more suffering than the poverty of the learned.

old: The unlearned, though born in a high caste, are not equal in dignity to the learned; though they may have been born in a low caste
modern: An uneducated person, even if born into a high caste, does not have the same dignity as an educated person, even if the educated person was born into a low caste.

old: As beasts by the side of men, so are other men by the side of those who are learned in celebrated works
modern: Beside those who are learned in celebrated works, other people are like beasts beside human beings.

old: Wealth (gained) by the ear is wealth of wealth; that wealth is the chief of all wealth
modern: The wealth of wealth is the wealth gained through listening, and this wealth is the best of all wealth.

old: When there is no food for the ear, give a little also to the stomach
modern: When there is no food for the ear, then give a little to the stomach as well.

old: Those who in this world enjoy instruction which is the food of the ear, are equal to the Gods, who enjoy the food of the sacrifices
modern: Someone who feeds their ears with good questions is equal to the gods who eat the food offered in sacrifices.

old: Although a man be without learning, let him listen (to the teaching of the learned); that will be to him a staff in adversity
modern: Even if someone is uneducated, they should listen to the teachings of the learned, because doing so provides a helpful support during times of weakness or adversity.

old: The words of the good are like a staff in a slippery place
modern: The words of a virtuous person are like a staff that helps you walk on slippery ground.

old: Let a man listen, never so little, to good (instruction), even that will bring him great dignity
modern: Listening to good things, even a little, will bring great dignity.

old: Not even when they have imperfectly understood (a matter), will those men speak foolishly, who have profoundly studied and diligently listened (to instruction)
modern: Those who have studied deeply and listened diligently will not speak foolishly, even when they have understood something imperfectly.

old: The ear which has not been bored by instruction, although it hears, is deaf
modern: An ear that has not been opened by instruction is deaf, even if it hears sound.

old: It is a rare thing to find modesty, a reverend mouth- with those who have not received choice instruction
modern: Modest, respectful speech is rarely found in those who have not received choice instruction.

old: What does it matter whether those men live or die, who can judge of tastes by the mouth, and not by the ear ?
modern: People who only experience the physical tastes of the mouth and cannot appreciate the aesthetic and emotional tastes heard through the ear have nothing to lose if they die, and nothing to gain if they live.

old: Wisdom is a weapon to ward off destruction; it is an inner fortress which enemies cannot destroy
modern: Wisdom is a weapon that prevents destruction and an inner fortress that enemies cannot destroy.

old: Not to permit the mind to go where it lists, to keep it from evil, and to employ it in good, this is wisdom
modern: Wisdom prevents the mind from wandering wherever it wants to go, removes evil, and guides it toward the good.

old: To discern the truth in every thing, by whomsoever spoken, is wisdom
modern: Wisdom is to discern the truth in everything, whoever has spoken it.

old: To speak so as that the meaning may easily enter the mind of the hearer, and to discern the subtlest thought which may lie hidden in the words of others, this is wisdom
modern: Wisdom is the ability to speak clearly and simply so that others easily understand your thoughts, and to carefully figure out the subtle meanings hidden in the words of others.

old: To secure the friendship of the great is true wisdom; it is (also) wisdom to keep (that friendship unchanged, and) not opening and closing (like the lotus flower)
modern: True wisdom is to befriend the great and remain steadfast in that friendship, not opening and closing like a lotus flower.

old: To live as the world lives, is wisdom
modern: Wisdom is to live as the world lives.

old: The wise are those who know beforehand what will happen; those who do not know this are the unwise
modern: The wise can foresee what will happen in the future, while the unwise cannot.

old: Not to fear what ought to be feared, is folly; it is the work of the wise to fear what should be feared
modern: It is foolishness to not fear what should be feared, and it is the duty of the wise to fear what should be feared.

old: No terrifying calamity will happen to the wise, who (foresee) and guard against coming evils
modern: People with the wisdom to foresee and guard against future troubles will not suffer terrifying or shocking misfortunes.

old: Those who possess wisdom, possess every thing; those who have not wisdom, whatever they may possess, have nothing
modern: Those who have wisdom have everything, and those who do not have wisdom have nothing, even if they possess things.

old: Truly great is the excellence of those (kings) who are free from pride, anger, and lust
modern: Truly great is the prosperity of rulers who are free from pride, anger and lust.

old: Avarice, undignified pride, and low pleasures are faults in a king
modern: A king commits a fault when he is greedy, has undignified pride, and finds joy in bad things.

old: Those who fear guilt, if they commit a fault small as a millet seed, will consider it to be as large as a palmyra tree
modern: People who fear disgrace will consider a fault as small as a millet seed to be as large as a palmyra tree, and will avoid committing it.

old: Guard against faults as a matter (of great consequence; for) faults are a deadly enemy
modern: A fault is a deadly enemy that destroys you, so you should protect yourself by guarding against it as if it were your most valuable treasure.

old: The prosperity of him who does not timely guard against faults, will perish like straw before fire
modern: Someone who does not guard against a fault before it arrives will lose their life like straw placed before a fire.

old: What fault will remain in the king who has put away his own evils, and looks after the evils of others
modern: A king who first corrects his own faults and then examines the faults of others has no fault.

old: The wealth of the avaricious man, who does not expend it for the purposes for which he ought to expend it will waste away and not continue
modern: The wealth of a stingy person who does not spend it on good deeds will be wasted and destroyed.

old: Griping avarice is not to be reckoned as one among other faults; (it stands alone - greater than all)
modern: The greed of a miser's heart is not counted as one fault among others; it is the worst of all faults.

old: Let no (one) praise himself, at any time; let him not desire to do useless things
modern: One should never boast about oneself or desire to do things that do not yield any benefit.

old: If (a king) enjoys, privately the things which he desires, the designs of his enemies will be useless
modern: If someone can secretly enjoy the things they love without others knowing about it, the plans of their enemies will fail.

chapter: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
old: Let (a king) ponder well its value, and secure the friendship of men of virtue and of mature knowledge
modern: Weigh their worth carefully and secure the friendship of people who are virtuous and mature in knowledge.

chapter: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
old: Let (a king) procure and kindly care for men who can overcome difficulties when they occur, and guard against them before they happen
modern: You should cherish and keep close the help of wise people who can remove your current troubles and protect you from future ones.

chapter: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
old: To cherish great men and make them his own, is the most difficult of all difficult things
modern: To cherish great people and make them your own is the most difficult of all difficult things.

chapter: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
old: So to act as to make those men, his own, who are greater than himself is of all powers the highest
modern: To associate with people who are greater than you and follow their guidance is the highest form of power.

chapter: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
old: As a king must use his ministers as eyes (in managing his kingdom), let him well examine their character and qualifications before he engages them
modern: A ruler uses ministers as eyes, so their character and qualifications should be examined well before they are engaged.

chapter: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
old: There will be nothing left for enemies to do, against him who has the power of acting (so as to secure) the fellowship of worthy men
modern: Someone who knows how to live with worthy friends has nothing to fear from enemies, because they will not be able to harm him.

chapter: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
old: Who are great enough to destroy him who has servants that have power to rebuke him ?
modern: Someone who has close advisors that scold and correct him when he does wrong cannot be defeated by any enemy.

chapter: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
old: The king, who is without the guard of men who can rebuke him, will perish, even though there be no one to destroy him
modern: A king who lacks people to criticize him and protect him will ruin himself even if he has no enemies to destroy him.

chapter: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
old: There can be no gain to those who have no capital; and in like manner there can be no permanence to
modern: Someone who has no capital cannot make a profit from trade, and someone who has no support cannot have stability.

chapter: Seeking the Aid of Great Men
old: It is tenfold more injurious to abandon the friendship of the good, than to incur the hatred of the many
modern: It is ten times worse to abandon the friendship of good people than to incur the hatred of many enemies.

old: (True) greatness fears the society of the base; it is only the low - minded who will regard them as friends
modern: Noble people fear the company of the base, but low-minded people embrace them as friends.

old: As water changes (its nature), from the nature of the soil (in which it flows), so will the character of men resemble that of their associates
modern: The nature of water changes according to the soil it flows through, and a person's wisdom changes according to the character of their associates.

old: The power of knowing is from the mind; (but) his character is from that of his associates
modern: A person's character comes from their mind, but how they are judged by others comes from the people they associate with.

old: Wisdom appears to rest in the mind, but it really exists to a man in his companions
modern: Wisdom seems to come from the mind, but it actually comes from the company a person keeps.

old: Chaste company is the staff on which come, these two things, viz, purity of mind and purity of conduct
modern: Purity of mind and purity of action both come from having pure company.

old: To the pure-minded there will be a good posterity By those whose associates are pure, no deeds will be done that are not good
modern: A pure mind leads to good descendants and fame, while a pure lineage ensures that no bad deeds are done.

old: Goodness of mind will give wealth, and good society will bring with it all praise, to men
modern: Goodness of mind brings wealth, and good companionship brings all praise.

old: Although they may have great (natural) goodness of mind, yet good society will tend to strengthen it.
modern: Even if a wise person already has great mental goodness, the good company of friends will further protect and strengthen it.

old: Future bliss is (the result) of goodness of mind; and even this acquires strength from the society of the good
modern: Goodness of mind brings future bliss, and this is strengthened by the company of good people.

old: There is no greater help than the company of the good; there is no greater source of sorrow than the company of the wicked
modern: There is no greater help than the company of the good, and no greater source of sorrow than the company of the wicked.

old: Let a man reflect on what will be lost, what will be acquired and (from these) what will be his ultimate gain, and (then, let him) act
modern: Before doing an action, a person should figure out what will be lost, what will be gained, and what the future reward will be, and then act. They should weigh the loss, the gain, and the reward of a deed before proceeding to do it.

old: There is nothing too difficult to (be attained by) those who, before they act, reflect well themselves, and thoroughly consider (the matter) with chosen friends
modern: There is nothing difficult to achieve for someone who carefully plans an action with trusted friends and then reflects on it themselves before doing it.

old: Wise men will not, in the hopes of profit, undertake works that will consume their principal
modern: Wise people do not undertake actions that risk losing their current capital just to gain more profit.

old: Those who fear reproach will not commence anything which has not been (thoroughly considered) and made clear to them
modern: Someone who fears being blamed will not start a task whose outcome is not clear.

old: One way to promote the prosperity of an enemy, is (for a king) to set out (to war) without having thoroughly weighed his ability (to cope with its chances)
modern: Going to war without thoroughly considering all the ways to act and the resulting outcomes is a way to plant an enemy in growing soil so he can thrive.

old: He will perish who does not what is not fit to do; and he also will perish who does not do what it is fit to
modern: Doing what is not fit to do causes ruin, and not doing what is fit to do also causes ruin.

old: Consider, and then undertake a matter; after having undertaken it, to say "We will consider," is folly
modern: A person should think and plan before starting a proper task, and it is wrong to say they will think about it after they have already started.

old: The work, which is not done by suitable methods, will fail though many stand to uphold it
modern: Effort without a proper method will fail, even if many people support it.

old: There are failures even in acting well, when it is done without knowing the various dispositions of men
modern: Even when trying to do good, mistakes happen if you do not understand people's individual natures and act accordingly.

old: Let a man reflect, and do things which bring no reproach; the world will not approve, with him, of things which do not become of his position to adopt
modern: A person should plan and perform actions that others will not despise, because the world will reject and mock actions that do not suit their status or position.

old: Let (one) weigh well the strength of the deed (he purposes to do), his own strength, the strength of his enemy, and the strength of the allies (of both), and then let him act
modern: One should weigh the strength of the task, one's own strength, the enemy's strength, and the strength of allies before acting.

old: There is nothing which may not be accomplished by those who, before they attack (an enemy), make themselves acquainted with their own ability, and with whatever else is (needful) to be known, and
modern: People who know their own strength and figure out exactly what they need to do before taking action will never face an impossible task.

old: There are many who, ignorant of their (want of) power (to meet it), have haughtily set out to war, and broken down in the midst of it
modern: Many people, ignorant of their own strength, start a task with great enthusiasm but fail and are destroyed in the middle of it.

old: He will quickly perish who, ignorant of his own resources flatters himself of his greatness, and does
modern: Someone who does not get along with others and does not know their own strength will quickly be destroyed.

old: The axle tree of a bandy, loaded only with peacocks' feathers will break, if it be greatly overloaded
modern: A cart loaded only with light peacock feathers will still break its axle if it is loaded far beyond what it can carry.

old: There will be an end to the life of him who, having climbed out to the end of a branch, ventures to go further
modern: Someone who climbs to the very tip of a branch and then tries to go further will lose their life. This is a warning against overreaching one's limits.

old: Let a man know the measure of his ability (to give), and let him give accordingly; such giving is the way to preserve his property
modern: A person should give to others only up to the limit of their ability, and giving in this measured way is the proper way to preserve their wealth.

old: Even though the income (of a king) be small, it will not cause his (ruin), if his outgoings be not larger than his income
modern: Even if income is small, there is no harm as long as spending is not excessive.

old: The prosperity of him who lives without knowing the measure (of his property), will perish, even while it seems to continue
modern: A person who does not know the limits of their wealth and lives beyond their means will eventually lose everything, even if their life initially seems prosperous.

old: The measure of his wealth will quickly perish, whose liberality weighs not the measure of his property
modern: Giving without considering one's own wealth will quickly destroy that wealth.

old: A crow will overcome an owl in the day time; so the king who would conquer his enemy must have (a suitable) time
modern: A crow can defeat an owl in broad daylight, so a king who wants to defeat his enemies must choose the right time to fight.

old: Acting at the right season, is a cord that will immoveably bind success (to a king)
modern: Acting according to the right season is a cord that binds success so it does not slip away.

old: Is there anything difficult for him to do, who acts, with (the right) instruments at the right time ?
modern: Is there anything difficult for someone who acts with the right tools at the right time?

old: Though (a man) should meditate (the conquest of) the world, he may accomplish it if he acts in the right time, and at the right place
modern: If you act at the right time and place, you can easily win even the whole world, even if that is your greatest ambition.

old: They who thoughtfully consider and wait for the (right) time (for action), may successfully meditate (the conquest of) the world
modern: Someone who wants to conquer the world waits patiently and without anxiety for the right time to act.

old: The self-restraint of the energetic (while waiting for a suitable opportunity), is like the drawing back of a fighting-ram in order to butt
modern: A powerful person waits for the right moment to act instead of attacking immediately, just as a fighting ram steps back to gather momentum before charging its enemy. This self-restraint is not due to fear, but a deliberate pause to build strength for a more effective strike.

old: The wise will not immediately and hastily shew out their anger; they will watch their time, and restrain it within
modern: The wise do not show their anger outwardly when someone harms them, but instead wait for the right time to act and keep their anger hidden inside.

old: If one meets his enemy, let him show him all respect, until the time for his destruction is come; when that is come, his head will be easily brought low
modern: If you see your enemy, bear with them patiently until their time of destruction arrives, and then their head will fall.

old: If a rare opportunity occurs, while it lasts, let a man do that which is rarely to be accomplished (but for such an opportunity)
modern: When a rare and perfect opportunity arises, one should immediately perform the hardest deeds.

old: At the time when one should use self-control, let him restrain himself like a heron; and, let him like it, strike, when there is a favourable opportunity
modern: Wait patiently like a heron when the time is not right, and strike decisively like its peck when the time is right.

old: Let not (a king) despise (an enemy), nor undertake any thing (against him), until he has obtained (a suitable) place for besieging him
modern: Do not start any action or despise your enemy until you have found a suitable place to completely surround them.

old: Even to those who are men of power and expedients, an attack in connection with a fortification will yield many advantages
modern: Even for those who are powerful and skilled in warfare, gaining an advantage by using a fortress will bring many benefits.

old: Even the powerless will become powerful and conquer, if they select a proper field (of action), and guard themselves, while they make war on their enemies
modern: Even the weak can win if they choose the right place, protect themselves, and attack their enemies.

old: If they who draw near (to fight) choose a suitable place to approach (their enemy), the latter, will have to relinquish the thought which they once entertained, of conquering them
modern: If someone chooses a good position to fight from, their enemies will lose the confidence they had in winning.

old: In deep water, a crocodile will conquer (all other animals); but if it leave the water, other animals will conquer it
modern: A crocodile prevails over other animals in deep water, but if it leaves the water, other animals will defeat it.

old: Wide chariots, with mighty wheels, will not run on the ocean; neither will ships that the traverse ocean, move on the earth
modern: Large chariots with strong wheels cannot run on the ocean, and ships that sail on the sea cannot run on land. One should choose the right tools for the right place.

old: You will need no other aid than fearlessness, if you thoroughly reflect (on what you are to do), and select (a suitable) place for your operations
modern: If you carefully plan your actions and choose the right place to do them, you will not need any help other than fearlessness.

old: The power of one who has a large army will perish, if he goes into ground where only a small army can act
modern: If a king with a large army attacks a smaller army in a place where only the smaller army can operate, the large army's morale and strength will be destroyed. Even a smaller army can defeat a larger one if it fights from a location that favors its size.

old: It is a hazardous thing to attack men in their own country, although they may neither have power nor a good fortress
modern: It is difficult to attack people in their own land, even if they have no fort or other strengths.

old: A fox can kill a fearless, warrior-faced elephant, if it go into mud in which its legs sink down
modern: A fox can kill a fearless elephant with a warrior's face if the elephant gets stuck in deep mud where its legs sink.

old: Let (a minister) be chosen, after he has been tried by means of these four things, viz,-his virtue, (love of) money, (love of) sexual pleasure, and tear of (losing) life
modern: A person's true character should be tested through their virtue, wealth, pleasure, and fear of death before they are chosen for a job. You should observe how they behave regarding morality, money, physical pleasure, and their own life to understand their true nature.

old: (The king's) choice should (fall) on him, who is of good family, who is free from faults, and who has the modesty which fears the wounds (of sin)
modern: Someone born into a good family, free from faults, and who feels shame at the thought of doing wrong is the one a king should trust. This person is of noble birth, has no faults, and is modest enough to fear the wounds of sin.

old: When even men, who have studied the most difficult works, and who are free from faults, are (carefully) examined, it is a rare thing to find them without ignorance
modern: Even deeply learned and faultless people are rarely found to be completely free of ignorance when examined closely.

old: Let (a king) consider (a man's) good qualities, as well as his faults, and then judge (of his character) by that which prevails
modern: Weigh a person's good qualities and faults, and judge them based on whichever is more abundant.

old: A man's deeds are the touchstone of his greatness and littleness
modern: A person's own actions are the true test for determining their greatness and their meanness.

old: Let (a king) avoid choosing men who have no relations; such men have no attachment, and thereforehave no fear of crime
modern: Do not choose people who have no family or relatives, because they have no worldly attachments and feel no shame in committing bad deeds.

old: To choose ignorant men, through partiality, is the height of folly.
modern: Choosing ignorant people for a position out of personal affection brings all kinds of ignorance and useless outcomes. This happens because the king or leader, relying on affection rather than knowledge, appoints the wrong people, leading to ignorance and failure.

old: Sorrow that will not leave even his posterity will come upon him chooses a stranger whose character he has not known
modern: Trusting an untried stranger without examining their character and background causes endless, inescapable troubles for a person and their descendants.

old: Let (a king) choose no one without previous consideration; after he has made his choice, let him unhesitatingly select for each such duties as are appropriate
modern: Do not trust anyone without thoroughly testing them, and once they are tested, confidently entrust them with suitable duties.

old: To make choice of one who has not been examined, and to entertain doubts respecting one who has been chosen, will produce irremediable sorrow
modern: Trusting someone without examining them and doubting someone after you have examined and trusted them both cause endless sorrow.

old: He should be employed (by a king), whose nature leads him to choose the good, after having weighed both the evil and the good in any undertaking
modern: Someone who naturally chooses the good after weighing both good and evil should be employed.

old: Let him do (the king's) work who can enlarge the sources (of revenue), increase wealth and considerately prevent the accidents (which would destroy it)
modern: A ruler should act to expand sources of wealth, increase prosperity, and identify and remove any obstacles that threaten it.

old: Let the choice (of a king) fall upon him who largely possesses these four things, love, knowledge, a clear mind and freedom from covetousness
modern: You should trust someone who has a strong love for their work, the knowledge to do it well, the confidence to carry it out, and a lack of greed for the rewards.

old: Even when (a king) has tried them in every possible way, there are many men who change, from the nature of the works (in which they may be employed)
modern: Even after being carefully examined and found suitable in every possible way, many people still change their minds or act differently when it is time to actually perform the task.

old: (A king's) work can only be accomplished by a man of wisdom and patient endurance; it is not of a nature to be given to one from mere personal attachment
modern: One should not assign a task to someone just because they are a favorite, but only to a person who knows how to do it and can handle any difficulties that arise.

old: Let (a king) act, after having considered the agent (whom he is to employ), the deed (he desires to do), and the time which is suitable to it
modern: One should carefully consider the qualifications of the person who will do the work, the nature of the task itself, and the right time to do it, and then proceed with the action.

old: After having considered, "this man can accomplish this, by these means", let (the king) leave with him the discharge of that duty
modern: After considering that this man can accomplish this work with these means, one should leave that task with him.

old: Having considered what work a man is fit for, let (the king) employ him in that work
modern: After finding out what work a person is suited for, assign them to that specific job. Once appointed, let them perform the tasks that match their abilities.

old: Prosperity will leave (the king) who doubts the friendship of the man who steadily labours in the discharge of his duties
modern: Wealth and prosperity will leave a king who doubts the friendship of a man who is always diligent in his duties.

old: Let a king daily examine the conduct of his servants; if they do not act crookedly, the world will not act crookedly
modern: A king must daily examine the actions of his servants, because if they do not act crookedly, the world will not act crookedly.

old: Even when (a man's) property is all gone, relatives will act towards him with their accustomed (kindness)
modern: Even when a person has lost all their wealth, only relatives will continue to show them their old kindness and maintain their relationship.

old: If (a man's) relatives remain attached to him with unchanging love, it will be a source of everincreasing wealth
modern: If a person has relatives who love them without fail, that will give them ever-increasing wealth.

old: The wealth of one who does not mingle freely with his relatives, will be like the filling of water in a
modern: The life of someone who does not mingle with relatives is like water filling a tank with no banks.

old: To live surrounded by relatives, is the advantage to be derived from the acquisition of wealth
modern: The benefit of acquiring wealth is living surrounded by relatives who are happy and close to you.

old: He will be surrounded by numerous relatives who manifests generosity and affability
modern: Someone who gives what is needed and speaks kindly will be surrounded by many relatives.

old: No one, in all the world, will have so many relatives (about him), as he who makes large gift, and does not give way to anger
modern: A person who gives generously and does not get angry will have more relatives than anyone else in the world.

old: The crows do not conceal (their prey), but will call out for others (to share with them) while they eat it; wealth will be with those who show a similar disposition (towards their relatives)
modern: When crows find food, they do not hide it but call their relatives to share it with them; similarly, wealth and good fortune belong only to those who share their wealth with their relatives.

old: Many relatives will live near a king, when they observe that he does not look on all alike, but that he looks on each man according to his merit
modern: When a king looks at people based on their individual merits instead of treating everyone the same, many relatives will stay close to him.

old: Those who have been friends and have afterwards forsaken him, will return and join themselves (to him), when the cause of disagreement is not to be found in him
modern: People who were once close friends but left for a specific reason will return and stay with him once that cause is gone.

old: When one may have left him, and for some cause has returned to him, let the king fulfil the object (for which he has come back) and thoughtfully receive him again
modern: When someone who left without a reason comes back with a specific motive, the king should fulfill that purpose, examine their intentions, and accept them back.

old: More evil than excessive anger, is forgetfulness which springs from the intoxication of great joy
modern: Forgetting oneself in great joy is worse than excessive anger.

old: Forgetfulness will destroy fame, even as constant poverty destroys knowledge
modern: Forgetting destroys fame just as constant poverty destroys knowledge.

old: Thoughtlessness will never acquire fame; and this tenet is upheld by all treatises in the world
modern: Thoughtless people cannot gain fame, and this is a conclusion accepted by all schools of thought.

old: Just as the coward has no defence (by whatever fortifications ha may be surrounded), so the thoughtless has no good (whatever advantages he may possess)
modern: Someone who is fearful finds no use in any fortress, just as someone who is forgetful finds no good in any high position.

old: The thoughtless man, who provides not against the calamities that may happen, will afterwards repent for his fault
modern: A person who fails to foresee and guard against future troubles will later regret his mistake.

old: There is nothing comparable with the possession of unfailing thoughtfulness at all times; and towards all persons
modern: There is no greater benefit than always maintaining an unfailing, unforgetting nature towards everyone.

old: There is nothing too difficult to be accomplished, if a man set about it carefully, with unflinching endeavour
modern: There is nothing too difficult to accomplish if you work carefully with an unfailing, unforgetting mind.

old: Let (a man) observe and do these things which have been praised (by the wise); if he neglects and fails to perform them, for him there will be no (happiness) throughout the seven births
modern: One should carefully perform actions that the wise praise. Anyone who ignores and fails to do them will find no happiness in any of their seven births.

old: Let (a king) think of those who have been ruined by neglect, when his mind is elated with joy
modern: When you are overwhelmed by joy, remember the people who were ruined in the past because of their own arrogance and neglect.

old: It is easy for (one) to obtain whatever he may think of, if he can again think of it
modern: It is easy to get what you want if you can keep thinking about it without forgetting.

old: To examine into (the crimes which may be committed), to show no favour (to any one), to desire to act with impartiality towards all, and to inflict (such punishments) as may be wisely resolved on,
modern: To investigate a crime without showing favoritism to anyone, and then to decide and carry out the appropriate punishment based on the law.

old: When there is rain, the living creation thrives; and so when the king rules justly, his subjects thrive
modern: All living creatures on earth depend on the rain to survive, and in the same way, the subjects depend on the king's just rule. If the rain fails, the creatures cannot live, and if the king's justice fails, the subjects cannot thrive.

old: The sceptre of the king is the firm support of the Vedas of the Brahmin, and of all virtues therein described
modern: A king's rule is the foundation for the Vedas and the virtues described by Brahmins, and it protects the world.

old: The world will constantly embrace the feet of the great king who rules over his subjects with love
modern: A ruler who governs his land with love and embraces his subjects will have the world constantly clinging to his feet. People will live by following the path of a good ruler who governs his people fairly and holds them close.

old: Rain and plentiful crops will ever dwell together in the country of the king who sways his sceptre with justice
modern: In a country ruled by a king who governs justly according to the scriptures, timely rains and abundant crops will always occur together.

old: It is not the javelin that gives victory, but the king's sceptre, if it do no injustice
modern: It is not the spear but the king's straight scepter that brings victory, provided that scepter does not do injustice. A ruler's victory comes from just governance rather than weapons, as long as their rule remains fair and does not oppress the people.

old: The king defends the whole world; and justice, when administered without defect, defends the king
modern: The king protects the entire earth, and justice protects him as long as he rules without making mistakes.

old: The king who gives not facile audience (to those who approach him), and who does not examine and pass judgment (on their complaints), will perish in disgrace
modern: A king who is hard of access to those seeking justice, does not investigate their complaints thoroughly, and rules without proper justice will ruin himself. He will fall into a lowly state and perish even without any enemies.

old: In guarding his subjects (against injury from others), and in preserving them himself; to punish crime
modern: A king's duty is to protect his subjects from harm, preserve them himself, and punish any wrongdoing without fearing blame.

old: For a king to punish criminals with death, is like pulling up the weeds in the green corn
modern: When a king executes cruel people to protect the good, it is like a farmer pulling up weeds to save the crops.

old: The king who gives himself up to oppression and acts unjustly (towards his subjects) is more cruel than the man who leads the life of a murderer
modern: A king who oppresses his subjects is more cruel than a murderer.

old: The request (for money) of him who holds the sceptre is like the word of a highway robber who stands with a weapon in hand and says "give up your wealth"
modern: A king who stands with a sceptre and asks his subjects for money is just like a highway robber who stands with a weapon and demands your wealth.

old: The country of the king who does not daily examine into the wrongs done and distribute justice, will daily fall to ruin
modern: A king who does not daily investigate wrongs and administer justice will see his kingdom fall into ruin day by day.

old: The king, who, without reflecting (on its evil consequences), perverts justice, will lose at once both his wealth and his subjects
modern: A king who rules without thinking about the consequences will lose both his wealth and his subjects.

old: Will not the tears, shed by a people who cannot endure the oppression which they suffer (from their king), become a saw to waste away his wealth ?
modern: The tears shed by people suffering under an unjust ruler and crying out in unbearable pain act as a tool that wears away and destroys the ruler's wealth.

old: Righteous government gives permanence to (the fame of) kings; without that their fame will have no endurance
modern: Righteous rule is what makes a king's fame last; without it, the king's fame will not endure.

old: As is the world without rain, so live a people whose king is without kindness
modern: A king who lacks kindness causes the same kind of suffering to his living subjects as a lack of rain causes to the world.

old: Property gives more sorrow than poverty, to those who live under the sceptre of a king without justice
modern: Being wealthy is more painful than being poor if you live under the rule of an unjust king. The sorrow of possessing wealth is worse than the sorrow of lacking it when living beneath a cruel, unjust ruler.

old: If the king acts contrary to justice, rain will become unseasonable, and the heavens will withhold their showers
modern: If a king rules unjustly, the seasons will change and the sky will not provide rain.

old: If the guardian (of the country) neglects to guard it, the produce of the cows will fail, and the men of six duties viz, the Brahmins will forget the vedas
modern: If the king fails to properly protect the country, the cows will give less milk and the Brahmins will forget their sacred texts. Without protection, the cows lose their milk yield, and the people who perform the six Vedic duties stop reciting the mantras, so sacrifices no longer take place.

old: He is a king who having equitably examined (any injustice which has been brought to his notice), suitably punishes it, so that it may not be again committed
modern: A king is someone who investigates a crime fairly and then punishes the offender in a way that prevents them from committing the same crime again.

old: Let the king, who desires that his prosperity may long remain, commence his preliminary enquires with strictness, and then punish with mildness
modern: To ensure long-lasting rule, a ruler should begin punishments with a show of severity but then carry them out with gentleness. This approach prevents fear and ensures the ruler's authority remains strong over time.

old: The cruel-sceptred king, who acts so as to put his subjects in fear, will certainly and quickly come to ruin
modern: If a fierce king rules by doing cruel deeds that make his subjects fear him, the king will certainly and quickly come to ruin.

old: The king who is spoken of as cruel will quickly perish; his life becoming shortened
modern: A king who is called cruel by his subjects will quickly lose his life and wealth.

old: The great wealth of him who is difficult of access and possesses a sternness of countenance, is like that which has been obtained by a devil
modern: The great wealth of someone who is difficult to see and has a harsh face is ruined by the evil gaze of a demon. Because such a person is unapproachable and unpleasant to look at, their wealth is wasted and serves no use to themselves or to others.

old: The abundant wealth of the king whose words are harsh and whose looks are void of kindness, will instantly perish instead of abiding long, with him
modern: The wealth of a ruler who is harsh in speech and unkind in appearance will quickly perish.

old: Severe words and excessive punishments will be a file to waste away a king's power for destroying (his enemies)
modern: Harsh words and excessive punishments wear away a king's strength to defeat his enemies.

old: The prosperity of that king will waste away, who without reflecting (on his affairs himself), commits them to his ministers, and (when a failure occurs) gives way to anger, and rages against them
modern: A king who does not consult his ministers and instead blames them with anger when things go wrong will see his wealth waste away every day.

old: The king who has not provided himself with a place of defence, will in times of war be seized with fear and quickly perish
modern: A king who does not build a fort in advance will become terrified and quickly perish when war comes.

old: The earth bears up no greater burden than ignorant men whom a cruel sceptre attaches to itself (as the ministers of its evil deeds)
modern: A cruel ruler relies on ignorant people as ministers, and there is no heavier burden for the earth than this.

old: The world exists through that greatest ornament (of princes), a gracious demeanour
modern: The world exists because of the great beauty known as a benign gaze, which resides only in the hearts of kings. Without this grace, the world would be destroyed.

old: The prosperity of the world springs from the kindliness, the existence of those who have no (kindliness) is a burden to the earth
modern: The world functions because of the kindness of those who have it, and those without it are a burden to the earth.

old: Of what avail is a song if it be inconsistent with harmony ? what is the use of eyes which possess no kindliness
modern: A song that is not in harmony is useless, and an eye that has no kindness is also useless.

old: Beyond appearing to be in the face, what good do they do, those eyes in which is no well-regulated kindness ?
modern: Eyes that are on the face but lack measured kindness are useless. They only appear to be eyes but serve no other purpose.

old: Kind looks are the ornaments of the eyes; without these they will be considered (by the wise) to be merely two sores
modern: Kind looks are the jewels for the eyes, and without them, the eyes are felt as sores.

old: They resemble the trees of the earth, who although they have eyes, never look kindly (on others)
modern: Someone who has eyes but does not show kindness is like a tree rooted in the earth. They have eyes but do not look kindly at others.

old: Men without kind looks are men without eyes; those who (really) have eyes are also not devoid of kind looks
modern: People who do not have a kind and compassionate gaze are like those without eyes, and people who have eyes are never without a kind gaze.

old: The world is theirs (kings) who are able to show kindness, without injury to their affairs, (administration of justice)
modern: The world belongs to those who can perform their duties without fail while still showing kindness. They have the right to the world because they can manage their responsibilities and remain compassionate at the same time.

old: Patiently to bear with, and show kindness to those who grieve us, is the most excellent of all dispositions
modern: The highest virtue is to patiently bear with and show kindness to those who harm you.

old: Those who desire (to cultivate that degree of) urbanity which all shall love, even after swallowing the poison served to them by their friends, will be friendly with them
modern: Someone who wants a charming and agreeable nature will drink poison given by a friend without showing any disgust, just to maintain a good relationship with them.

old: Let a king consider as his eyes these two things, a spy and a book (of laws) universally esteemed
modern: A king should consider a spy and a book of laws as his two eyes.

old: It is the duty of a king to know quickly (by a spy) what all happens, daily, amongst all men.
modern: It is a king's duty to quickly learn through spies about everything that happens every day among all people, including friends, enemies, and the general public.

old: There is no way for a king to obtain conquests, who knows not the advantage of discoveries made by a spy
modern: A king who does not use spies to learn about events and their consequences cannot achieve victory. There is no other way for him to obtain conquests.

old: He is a spy who watches all men, to wit, those who are in the king's employment, his relatives, and his enemies
modern: A spy is someone who closely watches the king's officers, relatives, and enemies to understand their thoughts and actions.

old: A spy is one who is able to assume an appearance which may create no suspicion (in the minds of others), who fears no man's face, and who never reveals (his purpose)
modern: Someone who can appear completely trustworthy and never shows fear, and who can keep secrets no matter what methods are used.

old: He is a spy who, assuming the appearance of an ascetic, goes into (whatever place he wishes), examines into (all, that is needful), and never discovers himself, whatever may be done to him
modern: Someone who disguises themselves as a monk to gather secrets and never reveals them, even under torture.

old: A spy is one who is able to discover what is hidden and who retains no doubt concerning what he has known
modern: A spy is someone who can discover hidden things and then know them without any doubt.

old: Let not a king receive the information which a spy has discovered and made known to him, until he has examined it by another spy
modern: You should verify information given by one spy by having another spy investigate it and compare the two accounts. Only after the details match should you accept the information as true.

old: Let a king employ spies so that one may have no knowledge of the other; and when the information of three agrees together, let him receive it
modern: A ruler should use spies so that they do not know each other, and only when three spies report the same thing should the ruler believe it.

old: Let not a king publicly confer on a spy any marks of his favour; if he does, he will divulge his own secret
modern: A king should not publicly reward a spy, because doing so will cause the spy to reveal the king's hidden secrets to outsiders.

old: Energy makes out the man of property; as for those who are destitute of it, do they (really) possess what they possess ?
modern: True ownership belongs to someone who has energy. Those who lack energy do not truly own anything, even if they possess other things.

old: The possession of (energy of) mind is true property; the possession of wealth passes away and abides not
modern: Having enthusiasm is the only lasting possession, while material wealth will not stay and will eventually leave.

old: They who are possessed of enduring energy will not trouble themselves, saying, "we have lost our property."
modern: People who have strong determination and self-control do not get upset or complain when they lose their wealth. Even if they lose their possessions, they do not lose their resolve or get distressed.

old: Wealth will find its own way to the man of unfailing energy
modern: Wealth will find its own way to the man of unfailing energy.

old: The stalks of water-flowers are proportionate to the depth of water; so is men's greatness proportionate to their minds
modern: The depth of the water determines the length of a lotus's stem, and similarly, a person's greatness is determined by their inner motivation. Just as a lotus grows taller in deeper water, a person's life rises in proportion to their mental drive.

old: In all that a king thinks of, let him think of his greatness; and if it should be thrust from him (by fate), it will have the nature of not being thrust from him
modern: One should always think great thoughts, and even if those thoughts do not come true, the act of thinking them is a virtue in itself.

old: The strong minded will not faint, even when all is lost; the elephant stands firm, even when wounded by a shower of arrows
modern: An elephant stands firm and keeps its dignity even when pierced by a shower of arrows, and in the same way, strong-minded people do not lose their resolve or greatness even when facing total ruin.

old: Those who have no (greatness of) mind, will not acquire the joy of saying in the world, "we have excercised liaberality"
modern: Someone who lacks enthusiasm or a generous spirit cannot experience the joy of being recognized in the world as a truly generous and noble person. Without this inner greatness, they will not acquire the proud feeling of being known for their charity.

old: Although the elephant has a large body, and a sharp tusk, yet it fears the attack of the tiger
modern: Although the elephant has a large body and a sharp tusk, it fears the attack of the tiger.

old: Energy is mental wealth; those men who are destitute of it are only trees in the form of men
modern: Mental courage is true manhood; without it, a person is just a tree.

old: By the darkness, of idleness, the indestructible lamp of family (rank) will be extinguished
modern: The family's honor, like an unquenchable lamp, will be extinguished when the darkness of idleness covers it.

old: Let those, who desire that their family may be illustrious, put away all idleness from their conduct
modern: If you want to make your family a great family, you should treat laziness as a true evil and work hard.

old: The (lustre of the) family of the ignorant man, who acts under the influence of destructive laziness will perish, even before he is dead
modern: The standing of the family of a foolish person who acts under destructive laziness will perish even before that person dies.

old: Family (greatness) will be destroyed, and faults will increase, in those men who give way to laziness, and put forth no dignified exertions
modern: When someone falls into laziness and makes no noble effort, their family is ruined and their faults multiply.

old: Procrastination, forgetfulness, idleness, and sleep, these four things, form the vessel which is desired by those destined to destruction
modern: Delaying tasks, forgetting them, feeling lazy, and sleeping too much are four things that people heading for ruin willingly board like a pleasure boat.

old: It is a rare thing for the idle, even when possessed of the riches of kings who ruled over the whole earth, to derive any great benefit from it
modern: Even if someone gains the wealth of all the world's rulers, a lazy person will not gain any real benefit from it.

old: Those who through idleness, and do not engage themselves in dignified exertion, will subject
modern: Someone who prefers laziness and avoids great effort will face mockery from their friends, who will first scold them for their useless excuses and later speak to them with contempt.

old: If idleness take up its abode in a king of high birth, it will make him a slave of his enemies
modern: If laziness takes up residence in a noble family, it will make them a slave to their enemies.

old: When a man puts away idleness, the reproach which has come upon himself and his family will disappear
modern: When a person stops being lazy, the disgrace that has come to their family and themselves will disappear.

old: The king who never gives way to idleness will obtain entire possession of (the whole earth) passed over by him who measured (the worlds) with His foot
modern: A king who is not lazy will gain control of the entire world that was measured by the god who stepped across it.

old: Yield not to the feebleness which says, "this is too difficult to be done"; labour will give the greatness (of mind) which is necessary (to do it)
modern: Do not feel discouraged by the difficulty of a task, because effort will give you the strength to accomplish it.

old: Take care not to give up exertion in the midst of a work; the world will abandon those who abandon their unfinished work
modern: The world abandons people who abandon their work before finishing it, so you should not leave a task incomplete. If you start a task, you must finish it because the world will abandon those who give up on their unfinished work.

old: The lustre of munificence will dwell only with the dignity of laboriousness or efforts
modern: The pride of helping others is firmly established in the noble quality of hard work. The desire to help people exists only in those who possess the dignity of strenuous effort.

old: The liberality of him, who does not labour, will fail, like the manliness of a hermaphrodite, who has a sword in its hand
modern: Someone who does not work hard will fail to be generous, just as a sword in the hand of a eunuch is useless.

old: He who desires not pleasure, but desires labour, will be a pillar to sustain his relations, wiping away their sorrows
modern: Someone who does not seek pleasure but instead desires to complete their work will wipe away the grief of their friends and family and become a pillar of support for them.

old: Labour will produce wealth; idleness will bring poverty
modern: Hard work brings wealth, and a lack of effort leads to poverty.

old: They say that the black Mudevi (the goddess of adversity) dwells with laziness, and the Latchmi (the goddess of prosperity) dwells with the labour of the industrious
modern: The goddess of adversity dwells with the lazy, while the goddess of prosperity dwells with the industrious.

old: Adverse fate is no disgrace to any one; to be without exertion and without knowing what should be known, is disgrace
modern: Adverse fate is no disgrace to anyone; not knowing what should be known and not doing one's work is the disgrace.

old: Although it be said that, through fate, it cannot be attained, yet labour, with bodily exertion, will yield its reward
modern: Even if divine fate prevents success, hard work and physical effort will still yield their own reward.

old: They who labour on, without fear and without fainting will see even fate (put) behind their back
modern: Someone who works tirelessly without ever giving up will eventually overcome even fate or bad karma and leave it behind.

old: If troubles come, laugh; there is nothing like that, to press upon and drive away sorrow
modern: When troubles come, you should laugh, because nothing is as effective as that at driving away sorrow and defeating the hardship.

old: A flood of troubles will be overcome by the (courageous) thought which the minds of the wise will entertain, even in sorrow
modern: A flood of troubles will be overcome by the thought of a wise person. The sorrow itself will disappear when the wise person considers its nature.

old: They give sorrow to sorrow, who in sorrow do not suffer sorrow
modern: Those who do not suffer sorrow when it comes will make sorrow itself suffer and will overcome it.

old: Troubles will vanish (i.e., will be troubled) before the man who (struggles against difficulties) as a
modern: Someone who struggles like a bull pulling a cart through difficult paths will cause their own troubles to disappear.

old: The troubles of that man will be troubled (and disappear) who, however thickly they may come upon him, does not abandon (his purpose)
modern: When troubles keep coming one after another, they will eventually destroy the person who is troubled by them. If a person remains steady and does not lose their resolve, the troubles that come will themselves be destroyed.

old: Will those men ever cry out in sorrow, "we are destitute" who, (in their prosperity), give not way to (undue desire) to keep their wealth
modern: People who do not cling to their wealth or grieve over their poverty will not worry when they lose their riches. Those who did not rejoice in their prosperity or try to hoard their wealth will not lament when they become destitute.

old: The great will not regard trouble as trouble, knowing that the body is the butt of trouble
modern: Wise people do not get disturbed by trouble, knowing that the body is naturally the target of suffering.

old: That man never experiences sorrow, who does not seek for pleasure, and who considers distress to be natural (to man)
modern: Someone who does not seek pleasure and considers suffering to be natural will not be harmed by sorrow.

old: He does not suffer sorrow, in sorrow who does not look for pleasure in pleasure
modern: Someone who does not get attached to pleasure will not be affected by pain. They do not seek pleasure in pleasure, nor do they get distressed by pain.

old: The elevation, which even his enemies will esteem, will be gained by him, who regards pain as pleasure
modern: Someone who sees pain as pleasure will gain a glory that even their enemies will admire.

chapter: The Office of Minister of state
old: The minister is one who can make an excellent choice of means, time, manner of execution, and the difficult undertaking (itself)
modern: A minister is someone who successfully chooses the right tools, the right time, the right way to do the work, and the rare or difficult task itself.

chapter: The Office of Minister of state
old: The minister is one who in addition to the aforesaid five things excels in the possession of firmness,
modern: A minister must possess firmness, the protection of people, learned wisdom, knowledge from learned people, and effort.

chapter: The Office of Minister of state
old: The minister is one who can effect discord (among foes), maintain the good-will of his friends and restore to friendship those who have seceded (from him)
modern: A minister is someone who can divide enemies, keep friends loyal, and reunite those who have separated.

chapter: The Office of Minister of state
old: The minister is one who is able to comprehend (the whole nature of an undertaking), execute it in the best manner possible, and offer assuring advice (in time of necessity)
modern: A minister is someone who can thoroughly understand a task, figure out the best ways to execute it, and firmly communicate the conclusions.

chapter: The Office of Minister of state
old: He is the best helper (of the king) who understanding the duties, of the latter, is by his special learning, able to tender the fullest advice, and at all times conversant with the best method (of
modern: Someone who understands righteousness, speaks with wisdom, and knows how to act at all times is the best helper.

chapter: The Office of Minister of state
old: What (contrivances) are there so acute as to resist those who possess natural acuteness in addition to learning ?
modern: What extremely clever schemes can stand against someone who possesses both natural intelligence and scholarly knowledge? Nothing can.

chapter: The Office of Minister of state
old: Though you are acquainted with the (theoretical) methods (of performing an act), understand the ways of the world and act accordingly
modern: Even if you know how to act from books, you should understand the ways of the world and act accordingly.

chapter: The Office of Minister of state
old: Although the king be utterly ignorant, it is the duty of the minister to give (him) sound advice
modern: A minister must firmly give sound advice to a king who is ignorant and ignores what is said, even if the king gets angry.

chapter: The Office of Minister of state
old: Far better are seventy crores of enemies (for a king) than a minister at his side who intends (his) ruin
modern: It is better to have seventy crores of enemies than a minister who plots harm from close by. Such a minister is worse than countless external foes.

chapter: The Office of Minister of state
