old: Those ministers who are destitute of (executive) ability will fail to carry out their projects, although they may have contrived aright
modern: People who lack the ability to execute will leave things incomplete, even if they have carefully planned them out.

old: The possession of that goodness which is called the goodness of speech is (even to others) better than any other goodness
modern: The ability to speak well is a special kind of wealth that is better than all other good things and cannot be found anywhere else.

old: Since (both) wealth and evil result from (their) speech, ministers should most carefully guard themselves against faultiness therein
modern: Since both good and bad results come from speech, one must guard against mistakes in what one says.

old: The (minister's) speech is that which seeks (to express) elements as bind his friends (to himself) and is so delivered as to make even his enemies desire (his friendship)
modern: Speech is the ability to speak in a way that binds those who have heard to you and makes even those who have not heard want to hear.

old: Understand the qualities (of your hearers) and (then) make your speech; for superior to it, there is neither virtue nor wealth
modern: Understand the qualities of the person you are speaking to before you speak. There is no higher virtue or greater wealth than choosing the right words for your audience.

old: Deliver your speech, after assuring yourself that no counter speech can defeat your own
modern: Speak your words only after confirming that no other words can defeat them.

old: It is the opinion of those who are free from defects in diplomacy that the minister should speak so as to make his hearers desire (to hear more) and grasp the meaning of what he hears himself
modern: People with spotless character speak in a way that makes others want to hear more, and they carefully grasp the true meaning of what others say.

old: It is impossible for any one to conquer him by intrique who possesses power of speech, and is neither faulty nor timid
modern: Someone who can speak persuasively, never gets tired of speaking, and is fearless cannot be defeated by an enemy.

old: If there be those who can speak on various subjects in their proper order and in a pleasing manner, the world would readily accept them
modern: If you have people who can organize their thoughts and speak them pleasantly, the world will quickly listen to their instructions and carry them out.

old: They will desire to utter many words, who do not know how to speak a few faultless ones
modern: Someone who cannot speak a few faultless words will want to speak many words.

old: Those who are unable to set forth their acquirements (before others) are like flowers blossoming in a cluster and yet without fragrance
modern: Someone who cannot explain what they have learned is like a flower that has bloomed in a cluster but has no fragrance.

old: The efficacy of support will yield (only) wealth; (but) the efficacy of action will yield all that is desired
modern: Friendship brings material wealth, but good actions provide everything else you desire.

old: Ministers should at all times avoid acts which, in addition to fame, yield no benefit (for the future)
modern: A person should always avoid actions that do not bring fame in this life and goodness in the next.

old: Those who say, "we will become (better)" should avoid the performance of acts that would destroy (their fame)
modern: People who want to achieve greatness should avoid doing things that ruin their reputation. They should not perform actions that dim their light of glory.

old: Those who have infallible judgement though threatened with peril will not do acts which have brought disgrace (on former ministers)
modern: Someone with clear judgment will not do shameful deeds, even if they are in great trouble.

old: Let a minister never do acts of which he would have to grieve saying, "what is this I have done"; (but) should he do (them), it were good that he grieved not
modern: Do not do things that make you regret and grieve later, and if you do make a mistake, do not repeat it.

old: Though a minister may see his mother starve; let him do not act which the wise would (treat with contempt)
modern: Even if you see your own mother starving, you should not do actions that wise people condemn.

old: Far more excellent is the extreme poverty of the wise than wealth obtained by heaping up of sinful
modern: It is better to live in severe poverty with a clear conscience than to be wealthy through sinful actions that bring a bad reputation.

old: The actions of those, who have not desisted from doing deeds forbidden (by the great), will, even if they succeed, cause them sorrow
modern: Even if forbidden actions succeed, they will ultimately cause sorrow to those who ignore the advice of good people and do them for wealth.

old: All that has been obtained with tears (to the victim) will depart with tears (to himself); but what has been by fair means; though with loss at first, will afterwards yield fruit
modern: Wealth obtained by making others cry will eventually be lost when the perpetrator themselves cries, but wealth gained through good deeds will bear fruit later even if it is lost first.

old: (For a minister) to protect (his king) with wealth obtained by foul means is like preserving a vessel of wet clay by filling it with water
modern: Trying to protect wealth gained through wrongdoing is like trying to store water in a pot made of wet clay.

old: Firmness in action is (simply) one's firmness of mind; all other (abilities) are not of this nature
modern: Firmness in action is simply firmness of mind; all other abilities are not of this nature.

old: Not to perform a ruinous act, and not to be discouraged by the ruinous termination of an act, are the two maxims which, the wise say, from the principles of those who have investigated the subject
modern: Do not start a harmful action, and do not give up if a harmful action you started fails. These two principles are what wise people who have studied the subject say.

old: So to perform an act as to publish it (only) at its termination is (true) manliness; for to announce it beforehand, will cause irremediable sorrow
modern: True manliness means doing an act so that it is only revealed at the end, because revealing it beforehand will cause irremediable sorrow.

old: To say (how an act is to be performed) is (indeed) easy for any one; but far difficult it is to do according to what has been said
modern: It is easy for anyone to say how to do something, but it is difficult to actually do it that way.

old: The firmness in action of those who have become great by the excellence (of their counsel) will, by attaining its fulfilment in the person of the king, be esteemed (by all).
modern: The firm resolve of great people, proven by their actions, will be highly valued by the king and everyone else.

old: If those who have planned (an undertaking) possess firmness (in executing it) they will obtain what they have desired even as they have desired it
modern: If people have the determination to execute their plans, they will achieve exactly what they intended to achieve.

old: Let none be despised for (their) size; (for) the world has those who resemble the linch-pin of the big rolling car
modern: Do not despise people just because of their small physical size, as there are people in the world who are like the small linchpin of a big rolling chariot that holds it all together.

old: An act that has been firmly resolved on must be as firmly carried out without delay
modern: Once you clearly resolve to do something, you must carry it out immediately without any hesitation, delay, or wavering.

old: Though it should cause increasing sorrow (at the outset), do with firmness the act that yield bliss (in the end)
modern: Even if a task causes great pain at first, you should do it with firm resolve because it will bring happiness in the end.

old: The great will not esteem those who esteem not firmness of action, whatever other abilities the latter may possess
modern: The world does not respect someone who lacks determination in their actions, even if they have many other strengths. A person without firmness in what they do will not be valued by the wise, no matter how capable they may be in other ways.

old: Consultation ends in forming a resolution (to act); (but) delay in the execution of that resolve is an evil
modern: After careful planning, one should make a firm decision to act, and delaying that action is a harmful mistake. If you hesitate after making up your mind, your enemies will notice, which will lead to your destruction.

old: Sleep over such (actions) as may be slept over; (but) never over such as may not be slept over
modern: Delay actions that can be delayed, but do not delay actions that must be done quickly.

old: Whenever it is possible (to overcome your enemy) the act (of fighting) is certainly good; if not, endeavour to employ some more successful method
modern: When it is possible to act, you should act. If it is not possible, you should look for another way to act.

old: When duly considered, the incomplete execution of an undertaking and hostility will grow and destroy one like the (unextinguished) remnant of a fire
modern: If you leave work or a conflict unfinished, the remaining parts will grow and destroy you like an unextinguished fire.

old: Do an act after a due consideration of the (following) five, viz money, means, time, execution and place
modern: Before you act, carefully consider five things: the resources you need, the tools you have, the right time, the method of execution, and the location. Each of these has two aspects, such as your own resources versus your opponent's.

old: An act is to be performed after considering the exertion required, the obstacles to be encountered, and the great profit to be gained (on its completion)
modern: Before starting an action, carefully consider the effort needed to finish it, the obstacles you will face, and the great profit you will gain once it is done. Only after weighing these factors should you go ahead and do the work.

old: The method of performance for one who has begun an act is to ascertain the mind of him who knows the secret thereof
modern: A person who begins a task should first understand the mind of someone who thoroughly knows the secret of that task, and only then should they proceed with the method.

old: To make one undertaking the means of accomplishing another (similar to it) is like making one rutting elephant the means of capturing another
modern: Use one action to accomplish another, just as one elephant is used to capture another.

old: One should rather hasten to secure the alliance of the foes (of one's foes) than perform good offices to one's friends
modern: It is more urgent to quickly make friends with your enemies than to do good deeds for your friends.

old: Ministers of small states, afraid of their people being frightened, will yield to and acknowledge their superior foes, if the latter offer them a chance of reconciliation
modern: Ministers of small states, fearing their people will be frightened, will submit to a stronger ruler if they are offered a chance to reconcile.

old: The qualification of an ambassador are affection (for his relations) a fitting birth, and the possession of attributes pleasing to royalty
modern: A good ambassador is someone who loves their family, is from a noble family, and has qualities that please the king.

old: Love (to his sovereign), knowledge (of his affairs), and a discriminating power of speech (before other sovereigns) are the three sine qua non qualifications of an ambassador
modern: An ambassador must have love for his king, knowledge of his affairs, and the ability to speak wisely. These three qualities are essential for someone who speaks for a ruler.

old: To be powerful in politics among those who are learned (in ethics) is the character of him who speaks
modern: Someone who is a master of all scriptures among other scholars, and who speaks words of victory to kings with spears.

old: He may go on a mission (to foreign rulers) who has combined in him all these three viz, (natural) sense, an attractive bearing and well-tried learning
modern: Someone who possesses natural intelligence, an attractive appearance, and well-researched knowledge is qualified to go on a mission as an ambassador.

old: He is an ambassador who (in the presence of foreign rulers) speaks briefly, avoids harshness, talks so as to make them smile, and thus brings good (to his own sovereign)
modern: A good envoy speaks concisely, avoids harsh words, and says things that make people happy, which benefits their own ruler.

old: He is an ambassador who having studied (politics) talks impressively, is not afraid of angry looks, and knows (to employ) the art suited to the time
modern: A good envoy is someone who is well-learned, fearless, and can speak persuasively to win over an enemy. He must also know the right strategy for the specific situation and time.

old: He is chief (among ambassadors) who understands the proper decorum (before foreign princes), seeks the (proper) occasion, knows the (most suitable) place, and delivers his message after (due)
modern: The best ambassador is one who understands his duty, considers the right time and place, and thinks carefully before delivering his message.

old: The qualifications of him who faithfully delivers his (sovereign's) message are purity, the support (of foreign ministers), and boldness, with truthfulness in addition to the (aforesaid) three
modern: A messenger must be pure, have support, and be bold, and must also be truthful.

old: He alone is fit to communicate (his sovereign's) reply, who possesses the firmness not to utter even inadvertently what may reflect discredit (on the latter)
modern: Someone who speaks for a king must be able to deliver the message without ever saying anything that could bring shame to the king, even by accident. This person must have the courage to remain firm and not utter any unworthy words.

old: He is the ambassador who fearlessly seeks his sovereign's good though it should cost him his life (to deliver his message)
modern: A true envoy is someone who delivers his king's message to another ruler without fearing for his own life, even if it means he will be killed.

chapter: Conduct in the Presence of the King
old: Ministers who serve under fickle-minded monarchs should, like those who warm themselves at the fire, be neither (too) far, nor (too) near.
modern: Ministers serving fickle kings should interact with them like people warming themselves by a fire, staying neither too far away nor too close.

chapter: Conduct in the Presence of the King
old: For ministers not to cover the things desired by their kings will through the kings themselves yield them everlasting wealth
modern: Someone who does not crave the things that kings desire will be given lasting wealth by those kings. This specifically applies to items like food, ornaments, and status, which kings highly value. By avoiding the desire for these specific things out of respect, the king will gladly grant them abundant wealth.

chapter: Conduct in the Presence of the King
old: Ministers who would save themselves should avoid (the commission of) serious errors for if the king's suspicion is once roused, no one can remove it
modern: Ministers who want to protect themselves should avoid serious mistakes, because once a ruler suspects them, it is very difficult for anyone to clear that suspicion.

chapter: Conduct in the Presence of the King
old: While in the presence of the sovereign, ministers should neither whisper to nor smile at others
modern: In the presence of powerful people, one should not whisper or exchange smiles with others.

chapter: Conduct in the Presence of the King
old: (When the king is engaged) in secret counsel (with others), ministers should neither over-hear anything whatever nor pry into it with inquisitive questions, but (wait to) listen when it is divulged (by
modern: When a ruler is speaking in secret with others, you should not eavesdrop or ask questions about what is being discussed, but only listen if the ruler chooses to reveal it.

chapter: Conduct in the Presence of the King
old: Knowing the (king's disposition and seeking the right time, (the minister) should in a pleasing manner suggest things such as are desirable and not disagreeable
modern: A minister should observe the king's mood, wait for the right time, and politely suggest only the necessary things that he will actually like to hear.

chapter: Conduct in the Presence of the King
old: Ministers should (always) give agreeable advice but on no occasion recommend useless actions, though requested (to do so)
modern: Speak useful things that the king likes, even if he does not ask, and never speak useless things, even if he asks.

chapter: Conduct in the Presence of the King
old: Ministers should behave in accordance with the (Divine) light in the person of kings and not despise them saying, "He is our junior (in age) and connected with our family!"
modern: Do not despise a king by saying he is young or a relative; instead, behave with him according to the glory of his position.

chapter: Conduct in the Presence of the King
old: Those whose judgement is firm will not do what is disagreeable (to the sovereign) saying (within
modern: People with clear judgment will not do things that displease the ruler, thinking they have already earned the ruler's favor.

chapter: Conduct in the Presence of the King
old: The (foolish) claim with which a minister does unbecoming acts because of his (long) familiarity (with the king) will ensure his ruin
modern: Someone who assumes they are an old friend and does inappropriate things will face ruin. This happens because their long familiarity gives them the mistaken confidence to overstep their bounds.

old: The minister who by looking (at the king) understands his mind without being told (of it), will be a perpetual ornament to the world which is surrounded by a never-drying sea
modern: Someone who understands what another person means just by looking at their face without them saying a word is an ornament to the world surrounded by the never-drying sea.

old: He is to be esteemed a god who is able to ascertain without a doubt what is within (one's mind)
modern: One should regard as a god the person who can understand another's thoughts without any doubt.

old: The king should ever give whatever (is asked) of his belongings and secure him who, by the indications (of his own mind) is able to read those of another
modern: A ruler should give away any of his resources or even his kingdom to secure the help of someone who can read another person's inner thoughts just by observing their facial expressions.

old: Those who understand one's thoughts without being informed (thereof) and those who do not, may (indeed) resemble one another bodily; still are they different (mentally)
modern: Someone who can understand another person's thoughts without them being spoken is different in intellect from someone who cannot, even if they look the same physically.

old: Of what use are the eyes amongst one's members, if they cannot by their own indications dive those of another ?
modern: If a person cannot understand another's thoughts from their facial expressions, what use are the eyes among their body parts? If someone still cannot figure out what is in a person's mind even after seeing their facial expressions, what good are the eyes?

old: As the mirror reflects what is near so does the face show what is uppermost in the mind
modern: The face shows what is in the mind just as a mirror shows what is in front of it.

old: Is there anything so full of knowledge as the face ? (No) it precedes the mind, whether (the latter is) pleased or vexed
modern: The face reveals a person's feelings before the mind does. There is nothing more knowledgeable than the face.

old: If the king gets those who by looking into his mind can understand (and remove) what has occurred (to him) it is enough that he stand looking at their face
modern: If someone can understand what is in a person's mind by looking at their face, it is enough for that person to simply stand in front of them.

old: If a king gets ministers who can read the movements of the eye, the eyes (of foreign kings) will (themselves) reveal (to him) their hatred or friendship
modern: Someone who can understand the different ways people look can tell if they are friendly or hostile just by looking at their eyes.

old: The measuring-rod of those (ministers) who say "we are acute" will on inquiry be found to be their (own) eyes and nothing else
modern: The measuring rod for those who claim to have sharp intellects is simply their own eyes, and nothing else.

chapter: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber
old: Let the pure who know the arrangement of words speak with deliberation after ascertaining (the nature of) the court (then assembled)
modern: Pure-minded people who know the nature of different words should carefully consider the nature of the audience and speak appropriately.

chapter: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber
old: Let the good who know the uses of words speak with a clear knowledge after ascertaining the time (suited to the court)
modern: Good people who understand the nature and grammar of words should carefully assess the time and setting before speaking so they can speak clearly without making mistakes in their words or meanings, and in a way that the listeners will enjoy.

chapter: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber
old: Those who undertake to speak without knowing the (nature of the) court are ignorant of the quality of words as well as devoid of the power (of learning)
modern: Someone who speaks in a council without understanding its nature does not know the quality of words and has no power of speech.

chapter: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber
old: Ministers should be lights in the assembly of the enlightned, but assume the pure whiteness of mortar (ignorance) in that of fools
modern: In the presence of the wise, one should appear as knowledgeable as they are. In the presence of the foolish, one should appear as simple as white mortar.

chapter: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber
old: The modesty by which one does not rush forward and speak in (an assembly of) superiors is the best among all (one's) good qualities
modern: Among all the good qualities a person can have, the best is the modesty of not speaking first in front of elders or people who are more knowledgeable.

chapter: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber
old: (For a minister) to blunder in the presence of those who have acquired a vast store of learning and know (the value thereof) is like a good man stumbling (and falling away) from the path (of virtue)
modern: Making a mistake in speech before someone who has deeply studied and understood vast fields of knowledge is like a good person stumbling and falling away from the path of virtue.

chapter: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber
old: The learning of those who have read and understood (much) will shine in the assembly of those who faultlessly examine (the nature of) words
modern: The education of someone who has learned and understood many books will shine clearly when they speak in the assembly of people who can examine words without any mistakes. The value of their learning is recognized by those who flawlessly understand the meaning of words.

chapter: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber
old: Lecturing to those who have the ability to understand (for themselves) is like watering a bed of plants that are growing (of themselves)
modern: Speaking to people who can understand for themselves is like watering a field of growing grain.

chapter: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber
old: Those who are able to speak good things impressively in an assembly of the good should not even forgetfully speak them in that of the low
modern: Someone who can speak good things persuasively in an assembly of good people should not even speak them in an assembly of the foolish.

chapter: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber
old: To utter (a good word) in the assembly of those who are of inferior rank is like dropping nectar on the ground
modern: Speaking good words in front of people who are not your own kind is like spilling ambrosia in a dirty courtyard.

old: The pure who know the classification of words having first ascertained the nature (of the court) will not (through fear) falter in their speech before the powerful body
modern: People who are pure and know the different types of words do not falter in their speech when speaking before powerful councils because they understand the nature of the assembly.

old: Those who can agreeably set forth their acquirements before the learned will be regarded as the most learned among the learned
modern: Someone who can clearly and fearlessly explain what they have learned to other scholars will be recognized as the greatest scholar of them all. They are able to make the learned truly understand what they are saying.

old: Many indeed may (fearlessly) die in the presence of (their) foes; (but) few are those who are fearless in the assembly (of the learned)
modern: Many people are willing to die without fear in battle, but few are those who can speak without fear in a council of the wise.

old: (Ministers) should agreeably set forth their acquirements before the learned and acquire more (knowledge) from their superiors (in learning)
modern: When in the company of learned people, explain what you have learned in a way that they will understand and accept, and then learn even more from those who are more knowledgeable than you.

old: In order to reply fearlessly before a foreign court, (ministers) should learn logic according to the rules (of grammar)
modern: Learn the rules of grammar and logic to reply fearlessly in a council.

old: What have they to do with a sword who are not valiant, or they with learning who are afraid of an intelligent assembly ?
modern: A sword is useless to those who are not brave, and books are useless to those who are afraid of a wise assembly.

old: The learning of him who is diffident before an assembly is like the shining sword of an hermaphrodite in the presence of his foes
modern: The knowledge of someone who is afraid to speak in an assembly is like a sharp sword in the hands of a eunuch on a battlefield. Even if the assembly and the sword are perfectly fine, they become useless because of the cowardice of the person holding them.

old: Those who cannot agreeably speak good things before a good assembly are indeed unprofitable persons inspite of all their various acquirements
modern: A person who cannot clearly and agreeably express good ideas to a wise assembly is useless, even if they have studied many books.

old: They who, though they have learned and understood, are yet afraid of the assembly of the good, are said to be inferior (even) to the illiterate
modern: Someone who has learned but is afraid to speak in a good assembly is considered inferior to an illiterate person.

old: Those who through fear of the assembly are unable to set forth their learning in an interesting manner, though alive, are yet like the dead
modern: Someone who is afraid to speak in an assembly and cannot express what they have learned is considered as good as dead, even if they are alive.

old: A kingdom is that in which (those who carry on) a complete cultivation, virtuous persons, and
modern: A country is where there is unfailing cultivation, virtuous people, and inexhaustible wealth.

old: A kingdom is that which is desire for its immense wealth, and which grows greatly in prosperity, being free from destructive causes
modern: A country is a land that is rich in immense wealth, free from destructive pests and calamities, and produces abundant crops. It is highly desirable to others because of its great resources and high yields.

old: A kingdom is that which can bear any burden that may be pressed on it (from adjoining kingdoms) and (yet) pay the full tribute to its sovereign
modern: A true nation can bear heavy burdens, such as refugees or the costs of war, and still fully pay its taxes to the king.

old: A kingdom is that which continues to be free from excessive starvation, irremediable epidemics, and destructive foes
modern: A country is one that is free from fierce famine, relentless disease, and destructive enemies.

old: A kingdom is that which is without various (irregular) associations, destructive internal enemies, and murderous savages who (sometimes) harass the sovereign
modern: A kingdom is one without various factions, destructive internal enemies, and murderous groups that harass the king.

old: The learned say that the best kingdom is that which knows no evil (from its foes), and, if injured (at all), suffers no diminution in its fruitfulness
modern: The best country is one that remains untouched by enemies, and even if it suffers harm, its wealth does not diminish.

old: The constituents of a kingdom are the two waters (from above and below), well situated hills and an undestructible fort
modern: A country's essential parts are two sources of water, a suitable mountain, streams flowing from it, and a strong fort. These are the five necessary elements for a kingdom, including water from above and below, a mountain with streams, and an indestructible fort.

old: Freedom from epidemics, wealth, produce, happiness and protection (to subjects); these five, the learned, say, are the ornaments of a kingdom
modern: A country's jewels are five: freedom from disease, wealth, abundant produce, happiness, and protection. These five are what make a kingdom beautiful.

old: The learned say that those are kingdom whose wealth is not laboured for, and those not, whose wealth is only obtained through labour
modern: A true land is one that naturally provides wealth without requiring hard work, whereas a land that only yields wealth through constant labor is not a true land.

old: Although in possession of all the above mentioned excellences, these are indeed of no use to a country, in the absence of harmony between the sovereign and the sujects
modern: Even if a country has all the good qualities mentioned, they are useless without harmony between the king and the subjects.

old: A fort is an object of importance to those who march (against their foes) as well as to those who through fear (of pursuers) would seek it for shelter
modern: A fort is valuable for those who attack their enemies and for those who fear attack and seek shelter.

old: A fort is that which has everlasting water, plains, mountains and cool shady forests
modern: A fort is a place that has clear water, open plains, a mountain, and a dense forest. These four natural features make up the defenses of a fort.

old: The learned say that a fortress is an enclosure having these four (qualities) viz, height, breadth, strength and inaccessibility
modern: A fortress must have height, breadth, strength, and difficult access. These four qualities are what define a fort according to the texts.

old: A fort is that which has an extensive space within, but only small places to be guarded, and such as can destroy the courage of besieging foes
modern: A fort should have a large interior space but only a small area that actually needs to be guarded, and it should be capable of destroying the morale of attacking enemies.

old: A fort is that which cannot be captured, which abounds in suitable provisions, and affords a position of easy defence to its inmates
modern: A fort is one that cannot be captured by enemies, has plenty of food, and is easy to defend for those inside.

old: A fort is that which has all (needful) things, and excellent heroes that can help it against destruction (by foes)
modern: A fort is strong when it has all necessary supplies and brave heroes who can protect it from outside attacks.

old: A fort is that which cannot be captured by blockading, assaulting, or undermining it
modern: A fort is strong enough that enemies cannot capture it by surrounding it, fighting it directly, or using deceit.

old: That is a fort whose inmates are able to overcome without losing their ground, even abler men who have besieged it
modern: A fort is one where the people inside can defeat the besieging army without ever leaving their position.

old: A fort is that which derives excellence from the stratagems made (by its inmates) to defeat their enemies in the battlefield
modern: A fort is a place that gains greatness by using clever tactics from within to defeat enemies at the start of a battle.

old: Although a fort may possess all (the above-said) excellence, it is, as it were without these, if its inmates possess not the excellence of action
modern: Even the most magnificent fort is useless if its defenders lack the skill to act in battle. A fortress provides no strength to people who do not know how to fight.

old: Besides wealth there is nothing that can change people of no importance into those of (some) importance
modern: There is nothing else but wealth that can turn someone who is not respected into someone who is respected and valued.

old: All despise the poor; (but) all praise the rich
modern: Everyone despises the poor and praises the wealthy. This happens because people tend to look down on those who lack wealth, while elevating those who have it.

old: The imperishable light of wealth goes into regions desired (by its owner) and destroys the darkness (of enmity therein)
modern: Wealth is an unfailing lamp that goes wherever you want and destroys the darkness of enmity.

old: The wealth acquired with a knowledge of the proper means and without foul practices will yield virtue and happiness
modern: Wealth acquired through the right means and without any wrongdoing will bring a person both virtue and happiness.

old: (Kings) should rather avoid than seek the accumulation of wealth which does not flow in with mercy and love
modern: One should reject wealth that is not accompanied by grace and love. This kind of wealth is considered a disgrace and should be cast away.

old: The spoils of slaughtered foes; these are the royal revenues
modern: The king's wealth consists of property that becomes ownerless, taxes on goods, and spoils taken from defeated enemies.

old: The child mercy which is borne by love grows under the care of the rich nurse of wealth
modern: Grace, which is born from love, is nurtured by wealth, which is like a rich nurse.

old: An undertaking of one who has wealth in one's hands is like viewing an elephant-fight from a hill-top
modern: Someone who has wealth in hand can start a task and complete it without fear or worry, just like watching an elephant fight from a safe hill.

old: Accumulate wealth; it will destroy the arrogance of (your) foes; there is no weapon sharper than it
modern: You should accumulate wealth, as there is no sharper weapon than it to destroy the arrogance of your enemies.

old: To those who have honestly acquired an abundance of riches, the other two, (virtue and pleasure) are things easy (of acquisition)
modern: People who honestly earn a lot of wealth will easily obtain virtue and pleasure.

old: The army which is complete in (its) parts and conquers without fear of wounds is the chief wealth of the king
modern: A complete army that conquers without fear of injury is the king's greatest wealth. This force is made up of all its essential parts, such as infantry, cavalry, elephants, and chariots.

old: Ancient army can alone have the valour which makes it stand by its king at the time of defeat, fearless of wounds and unmindful of its reduced strength
modern: The bravery of a native army that stands fearless against wounds and defeat to protect its king cannot be found in hired or foreign forces.

old: What if (a host of) hostile rats roar like the sea ? They will perish at the mere breath of the cobra
modern: Even if a huge army of weak enemies makes a lot of noise, they will be destroyed by a single strong warrior.

old: That indeed is an army which has stood firm of old without suffering destruction or deserting (to the enemy)
modern: An army is one that has inherited courage from its ancestors and has never been destroyed or routed in battle. It is not shamed by defeats or desertions and has never been conquered by enemies.

old: That indeed is an army which is capable of offering a united resistance, even if Yama advances against it with fury
modern: An army is one that can stand united and resist even when death itself attacks.

old: Valour, honour, following in the excellent-footsteps (of its predecessors) and trust-worthiness; these four alone constitute the safeguard of an army
modern: An army is protected by four qualities: valour, honour, following the good path of predecessors, and being trusted by the king. These four are the army's safeguard.

old: That is an army which knowing the art of warding off an impending struggle, can bear against the dust-van (of a hostile force)
modern: An army knows how to withstand an enemy's attack and advances to face their vanguard without letting the dust of their approaching troops cover it.

old: Though destitute of courage to fight and strength (to endure), an army may yet gain renown by the splendour of its appearance
modern: Even if an army lacks the courage to fight and the strength to endure, it can still gain fame through the splendor of its appearance.

old: An army can triumph (over its foes) if it is free from diminution; irremediable aversion and poverty
modern: An army will win if it is free from weakness, lingering resentment, and poverty.

old: Though an army may contain a large number of permanent soldiers, it cannot last if it has no generals
modern: Even if an army has many permanent soldiers, it will not last without leaders.

old: O my foes, stand not before my leader; (for) many are those who did so but afterwards stood (in the shape of) statues
modern: O enemies, do not stand against my leader, because many who did so before have now turned into stone statues.

old: It is more pleasant to hold the dart that has missed an elephant than that which has hit hare in the forest
modern: It is better to hold a spear that missed an elephant than one that hit a hare.

old: The learned say that fierceness (incontest with a foe) is indeed great valour; but to become a benefactor in case of accident (to a foe) is the extreme (limit) of that valour
modern: Great valour is shown by fighting fiercely against an enemy, and the highest form of that valour is to help an enemy who has fallen into misfortune.

old: The hero who after casting the lance in his hand on an elephant, comes (in search of another) will pluck the one (that sticks) in his body and laugh (exultingly)
modern: A warrior who throws his spear at an elephant and then goes to find another will laugh and pull the spear from his own chest.

old: Is it not a defeat to the valiant to wink and destroy their ferocious look when a lance in cast at them (by their foe) ?
modern: It is a defeat for a brave person to close their eyes when an enemy throws a spear at them.

old: The hero will reckon among wasted days all those on which he had not received severe wounds
modern: A brave person will count their past days and consider any day without severe battle wounds on the face or chest to be completely wasted. They believe that a life without such scars is a life of uselessness.

old: The fastening of ankle-ring by those who disire a world-wide renown and not (the safety of) their lives is like adorning (themselves)
modern: Warriors who desire widespread fame and do not care about their own lives look beautiful when they wear anklets. These anklets represent heroic struggles, and the loud jingling they make loudly announces their names and fame to the world.

old: The heroes who are not afraid of losing their life in a contest will not cool their ardour, even if the king prohibits (their fighting)
modern: Brave warriors who are not afraid to risk their lives in battle will not lose their fierce spirit, even if their king angrily tells them to stop.

old: Who would reproach with failure those who seal their oath with their death ?
modern: Who would blame someone who dies in battle for keeping their vow?

old: If (heroes) can so die as to fill with tears the eyes of their rulers, such a death deserves to be obtained even by begging
modern: It is a great honor to beg for and obtain a heroic death that brings tears to the eyes of the ruler who protected you.

old: What things are there so difficult to acquire as friendship ? What guards are there so difficult to break through by the efforts (of one's foes) ? .
modern: What is as hard to acquire as friendship? What guards against the attacks of enemies are as hard to break through?

old: The friendship of the wise waxes like the new moon; (but) that of fools wanes like the full moon
modern: The friendship of wise people grows day by day like the waxing moon, while the friendship of fools fades away like the waning full moon.

old: Like learning, the friendship of the noble, the more it is cultivated, the more delightful does it become
modern: The more you interact with people of good character, the more delightful their friendship becomes, just as the more you read a book, the more you enjoy its meaning.

old: Friendship is to be practised not for the purpose of laughing but for that of being beforehand in giving one another sharp rebukes in case of transgression
modern: Friendship is not for laughing together but for correcting each other when they go too far.

old: Living together and holding frequent intercourse are not necessary (for friendship); (mutual) understanding can alone create a claim for it
modern: Living together and frequent interaction are not necessary for friendship; a shared feeling alone creates the bond.

old: The love that dwells (merely in the smiles of the face is not friendship; (but) that which dwells deep in the smiles of the heart is true friendship
modern: True friendship is not a smile on the face, but a smile in the heart.

old: (True) friendship turns aside from evil (ways) makes (him) walk in the (good) way, and, in case of loss if shares his sorrow (with him)
modern: True friendship prevents someone from going down a destructive path, guides them toward a good one, and shares their suffering when they face ruin.

old: (True) friendship hastens to the rescue of the afflicted (as readily) as the hand of one whose garment is loosened (before an assembly)
modern: True friendship is like a hand that immediately helps someone whose clothes are slipping, quickly removing their distress.

old: Friendship may be said to be on its throne when it possesses the power of supporting one at all times and under all circumstances, (in the practice or virtue and wealth)
modern: True friendship is when someone supports you with unwavering strength and without any change in their mind, especially in matters of virtue and wealth.

old: Though friends may praise one another saying, "He is so intimate with us, and we so much (with him)"; (still) such friendship will appear mean
modern: If friends boast about each other by saying, "He is so intimate with us, and we so much with him," that friendship will become worthless.

old: As those who are of a friendly nature will not forsake (a friend) after once loving (him), there is no evil so great as contracting a friendship without due inquiry
modern: Making an untested person your friend is the worst thing you can do, because once you form a friendship, you cannot easily break it.

old: The friendship contracted by him who has not made repeated inquiry will in the end grieve (him) to death
modern: Friendship formed without repeatedly testing a person's character and actions will ultimately cause grief that leads to death.

old: Make friendship (with one) after ascertaining (his) character, birth, defects and the whole of one's relations
modern: Before making a friend, you should carefully examine their character, family background, faults, and their close associates. Only after understanding these things should you become friends with them.

old: The friendship of one who belongs to a (good) family and is afraid of (being charged with) guilt, is worth even purchasing
modern: You should make friends with someone born into a noble family who feels ashamed of disgrace and avoids guilt, even if you have to pay a high price to do so.

old: You should examine and secure the friendship of those who can speak so as to make you weep over a crime (before its commission) or rebuke you severely (after you have done it) and are able to teach
modern: You should choose as friends those who can make you weep by warning you against wrongdoing before you commit it and by rebuking you after you have done it, and who can also teach you the right way to live.

old: Even in ruin there is some good; (for) it is a rod by which one may measure fully (the affection of one's) relations
modern: Even in ruin, there is a benefit: it is a rod that measures the true nature of one's friends.

old: It is indead a gain for one to renounce the friendship of fools
modern: It is truly a gain for someone to give up the friendship of fools.

old: Do not think of things that discourage your mind, nor contract friendship with those who would forsake you in adversity
modern: Do not think about actions that make your spirit shrink, and do not make friends with people who will abandon you when you are in trouble.

old: The very thought of the friendship of those who have deserted one at the approach of adversity will burn one's mind at the time of death
modern: The memory of friends who abandon you when you are in trouble will burn your mind even at the time of death.

old: Continue to enjoy the friendship of the pure; (but) renounce even with a gift, the friendship of those who do not agree (with the world)
modern: You should make friends with people who are free of blame and agree with the world, but you should give up the friendship of those who do not agree with the world even if you have to pay a price for it.

old: Imtimate friendship is that which cannot in the least be injured by (things done through the) right (of longstanding intimacy)
modern: True friendship is one that accepts the liberties taken by long-standing friends without ever rejecting or diminishing them.

old: The constituents of friendship are (things done through) the right of intimacy; to be pleased with such a right is the duty of the wise
modern: True friendship is shown through the right of intimacy, and it is the duty of the wise to be pleased by such actions.

old: Of what avail is long-standing friendship, if friends do not admit as their own actions done through the right of intimacy ?
modern: Long-standing friendship is useless if a friend does not accept your actions as their own when you act with the right of intimacy. If they do not agree to treat your actions as if they had done them themselves, then the friendship has no benefit.

old: If friends, through the right of friendship, do (anything) without being asked, the wise will be pleased with them on account of its desirability
modern: When close friends do familiar things unasked, the wise will gladly accept and appreciate their actions.

old: If friends should perform what is painful, understand that it is owing not only to ignorance, but also to the strong claims of intimacy
modern: If friends do something hurtful, understand that it is caused either by their ignorance or by their deep sense of intimacy.

old: Those who stand within the limits (of true friendship) will not even in adversity give up the intimacy of long-standing friends
modern: Someone who stays within the limits of true friendship will not abandon their connection with long-standing friends, even if it causes them harm or loss.

old: Those who have (long) stood in the path of affection will not give it up even if their friends cause (them) their ruin
modern: True friends who have long stood in the path of affection will not give up their love even if their friends cause them their ruin.

old: To those who understand that by which they should not listen to (tales about) the faults of their friends, that is a (profitable) day on which the latter may commit a fault
modern: For people who have the right to ignore the faults of their close friends even when others point them out, any day their friend makes a mistake is a good day.

old: They will be loved by the world, who have not forsaken the friendship of those with whom they have kept up an unbroken long-standing intimacy
modern: The world will love someone who does not abandon the friendship of those with whom they have had a long-standing, unbroken intimacy.

old: Even enemies will love those who have never changed in their affection to their long-standingfriends
modern: Even enemies will love someone who never changes their good nature and affection toward their old friends, even if those friends make mistakes.

old: The decrease of friendship with those who look as if they would eat you up (through excess of love) while they are really destitute of goodness is far better than its increase
modern: It is better for the friendship of people who lack good character to decrease, even if they appear to be extremely affectionate and eager to consume you, rather than for it to increase.

old: Of what avail is it to get or lose the friendship of those who love when there is gain and leave when there is none ?
modern: What is the use of gaining or losing the friendship of people who only stick around when they benefit from you and leave when they do not?

old: Friendship who calculate the profits (of their friendship), prostitutes who are bent on obtaining their gains, and thieves are (all) of the same character
modern: Friends who only care about the benefits they can get from a relationship, prostitutes who accept payment without any real affection, and thieves are all the same kind of people.

old: Solitude is more to be desired than the society of those who resemble the untrained horses which throw down (their riders) in the fields of battle
modern: It is better to be alone than to have the company of foolish people who abandon you in a crisis, just like an untrained horse that throws its rider during a battle.

old: It is far better to avoid that to contract the evil friendship of the base who cannot protect (their friends) even when appointed to do so
modern: It is better to avoid the friendship of lowly people who cannot protect you even if you help them.

old: The hatred of the wise is ten-million times more profitable than the excessive intimacy of the fool
modern: The hatred of a wise person is a hundred million times better than the close friendship of a fool.

old: What comes from enemies is a hundred million times more profitable than what comes from the friendship of those who cause only laughter
modern: You gain ten crore times more good from your enemies than from friends who are just vain laughers.

old: Gradually abandon without revealing (beforehand) the friendship of those who pretend inability to carry out what they (really) could do
modern: If friends pretend they cannot do a task they are actually capable of doing and ruin it, you should gradually abandon them without telling them.

old: The friendship of those whose actions do not agree with their words will distress (one) even in (one's) dreams
modern: The friendship of those whose actions do not match their words will cause distress even in dreams.

old: Avoid even the least approach to a contraction of friendship with those who would love you in private but ridicule you in public
modern: Do not associate with people who are friendly when you are alone at home but slander you in public gatherings.

old: The friendship of those who behave like friends without inward affection is a weapon that may be thrown when a favourable opportunity presents itself
modern: The friendship of people who pretend to be friends without actually liking you inside is like an anvil. They will use it to strike you down when they find a good opportunity to do so.

old: The friendship of those who seem to be friends while they are not, will change like the love of women
modern: The friendship of those who pretend to be kin but are not is fickle like a woman's mind.

old: Though (one's) enemies may have mastered many good books, it will be impossible for them to become truly loving at heart
modern: Even if someone has learned many good things, it is very difficult for a person with a bad heart to become good.

old: One should fear the deceitful who smile sweetly with their face but never love with their heart
modern: One should fear deceitful people who smile sweetly at you but harbor harmful intentions in their hearts.

old: In nothing whatever is it proper to rely on the words of those who do not love with their heart
modern: You should not trust the words of someone whose mind is not in harmony with yours, as their words cannot be relied upon in any matter.

old: Though (one's) foes may utter good things as though they were friends, once will at once understand (their evil, import)
modern: Even if enemies speak good things like friends, their true nature is quickly recognized.

old: Since the bending of the bow bespeaks evil, one should not accept (as good) the humiliating speeches of one's foes
modern: Do not trust the humble words of your enemies, as they are like a bent bow that signals harm.

old: A weapon may be hid in the very hands with which (one's) foes adore (him) (and) the tears they shed are of the same nature
modern: A weapon can be hidden in the very hands of enemies who bow to you, and their tears are just as deceptive.

old: It is the duty of kings to affect great love but make it die (inwardly); as regard those foes who shew them great friendship but despise them (in their heart)
modern: When enemies outwardly show great friendship but inwardly despise you, you should pretend to be friendly with them and make them outwardly happy so that their inner hatred fades away.

old: When one's foes begin to affect friendship, one should love them with one's looks, and, cherishing no love in the heart, give up (even the former)
modern: When your enemies pretend to be friends, you should smile at them but not trust them in your heart. If they later become truly friendly, you should also give up that friendship.

old: Folly is one (of the chief defects); it is that which (makes one) incur loss and forego gain
modern: Folly is the choice to accept things that bring harm while letting go of things that bring gain. It is the act of choosing loss over profit and harm over good.

old: The greatest folly is that which leads one to take delight in doing what is forbidden
modern: The greatest folly is to take delight in doing what is forbidden.

old: Shamelessness indifference (to what must be sought after), harshness, and aversion for everything (that ought to be desired) are the qualities of the fool
modern: Shamelessness, aimlessness, lovelessness, and not cherishing anything are the qualities of a fool.

old: There are no greater fools than he who, though he has read and understood (a great deal) and even taught it to others, does not walk according to his own teaching
modern: There is no greater fool than someone who reads and understands teachings, explains them to others, but does not follow them himself.

old: A fool can procure in a single birth a hell into which he may enter and suffer through all the seven births
modern: A foolish person who acts alone in a single lifetime can create a hell for themselves, into which they will sink and suffer across all seven future births.

old: If the fool, who knows not how to act undertakes a work, he will (certainly) fail (But) is it all ? He will even adorn himself with fetters
modern: When a fool who doesn't know the right way starts a task, not only does the task fail, but he also gets into trouble.

old: If a fool happens to get an immense fortune, his neighbours will enjoy it while his relations starve
modern: When a foolish person acquires great wealth, strangers and neighbors feast on it while his own relatives starve.

old: A fool happening to possess something is like the intoxication of one who is (already) giddy
modern: When a fool gets something, he is like a person who is already drunk and then drinks more alcohol.

old: The friendship between fools is exceedingly delightful (to each other): for at parting there will be
modern: Friendship with fools is very pleasant because parting from them does not bring any sorrow.

old: The appearance of a fool in an assembly of the learned is like placing (one's) unwashed feet on a bed
modern: A fool entering a gathering of wise people is like placing unwashed feet on a bed.

old: The want of wisdom is the greatest of all wants; but that of wealth the world will not regard as such
modern: The lack of wisdom is the greatest of all lacks, but the world does not consider the lack of wealth to be a lack at all.

old: (The cause of) a fool cheerfully giving (something) is nothing else but the receiver's merit (in a former birth)
modern: When a fool gives something with a happy heart, it is only because the receiver has good karma from a past life.

old: The suffering that fools inflict upon themselves is hardly possible even to foes
modern: Fools inflict a kind of suffering on themselves that even their enemies would not.

old: What is called want of wisdom is the vanity which says, "We are wise"
modern: Stupidity is the arrogance of thinking you are wise.

old: Fools pretending to know what has not been read (by them) will rouse suspicion even as to what they have thoroughly mastered
modern: Someone who pretends to know what they have not learned will cause others to doubt even what they actually do know.

old: Even to cover one's nakedness would be folly, if (one's) faults were not covered (by forsaking them)
modern: Fools try to hide their nakedness with clothes while failing to cover their inner faults. Trying to hide one's body is foolish if one does not first remove one's faults.

old: The fool who neglects precious counsel does, of his own accord, a great injury to himself
modern: A fool who neglects sacred teachings brings great harm upon himself.

old: The fool will not perform (his duties) even when advised nor ascertain them himself; such a soul is a
modern: Someone who does not do good things even when advised and does not understand them on their own is a plague to the world until they die.

old: One who would teach a fool will (simply) betray his folly; and the fool would (still) think himself "wise in his own conceit"
modern: Someone who tries to teach a foolish person who lacks knowledge will be considered ignorant himself, while the foolish person will just think he is wise based on the little he knows.

old: He who denies the existence of what the world believes in will be regarded as a demon on earth
modern: Someone who denies the existence of things that wise and good people clearly affirm, even when proven by evidence, will be considered a demon or ghost on earth.

old: The disease which fosters the evil of disunion among all creatures is termed hatred by the wise
modern: Hatred is a disease that creates a lack of harmony among all living beings and fosters the bad quality of disunion.

old: Though disagreeable things may be done from (a feeling of) disunion, it is far better that nothing painful be done from (that of) hatred
modern: Even if someone who is not on your side does hateful things, it is better not to do hateful things back to them.

old: To rid one-self of the distressing dtsease of hatred will bestow (on one) a never-decreasing imperishable fame
modern: If a person removes the painful disease of hatred from their mind, it will give them imperishable and lasting fame.

old: If hatred which is the greatest misery is destroyed, it will yield the greatest delight
modern: If hatred, which is the greatest misery, is destroyed, it will yield the greatest delight.

old: Who indeed would think of conquering those who naturally shrink back from hatred ?
modern: No one can defeat people who do not hold onto anger or hatred. They are the ones who cannot be conquered.

old: Failure and ruin are not far from him who says it is sweet to excel in hatred
modern: The life of someone who thinks it is sweet to have enmity with others is near failure and ruin. Their life is also near poverty and death.

old: Those whose judgement brings misery through its connection with hatred cannot understand the triumphant nature of truth.
modern: People who have a hateful mind cannot understand the truth that leads to victory.

old: Shrinking back from hatred will yield wealth; indulging in its increase will hasten ruin
modern: Turning away from enmity is a gain, but actively encouraging it brings fast ruin.

old: At the approach of wealth one will not think of hatred (but) to secure one's ruin, one will look to its increase
modern: When good fortune arrives, a person does not think of hatred, but when they are seeking their own ruin, they will think of increasing it.

old: All calamities are caused by hatred; but by the delight (of friendship) is caused the great wealth of good virtues
modern: All evils come from enmity, and all goodness comes from friendship.

old: Avoid offering resistance to the strong; (but) never fail to cherish enmity towards the weak
modern: Avoid fighting against those who are stronger than you, but actively seek out enmity with those who are weaker.

old: How can he who is unloving, destitute of powerful aids, and himself without strength overcome the might of his foe ?
modern: Someone who has no love for his relatives, lacks powerful allies, and has no strength of his own cannot defeat a strong enemy.

old: In the estimation of foes miserably weak is he, who is timid, ignorant, unsociable and niggardly
modern: Someone who is timid, ignorant, unsociable, and stingy is very easy for enemies to defeat.

old: He who neither refrains from anger nor keeps his secrets will at all times and in all places be easily conquered by all
modern: Someone who does not let go of their anger and cannot keep secrets will always and everywhere be an easy target for anyone.

old: (A) pleasing (object) to his foes is he who reads not moral works, does nothing that is enjoined by them cares not for reproach and is not possessed of good qualities
modern: Someone who does not follow the right path, does not do what is appropriate, does not fear blame, and lacks good qualities is easily defeated by his enemies.

old: Highly to be desired is the hatred of him whose anger is blind, and whose lust increases beyond measure
modern: It is actually good to be hated by someone who is blinded by anger and whose lust keeps growing. People will gladly accept the enmity of a person who acts without thinking and is consumed by endless desire.

old: It is indeed necessary to obtain even by purchase the hatred of him who having begun (a work) does what is not conductive (to its accomplishment)
modern: If someone who started a task does things that ruin it, you must secure their enmity even if it costs you some wealth. You should not hesitate to pay a price to make an enemy of someone who acts against the good of a shared endeavor.

old: He will become friendless who is without (any good) qualities and whose faults are many; (such a character) is a help to (his) foes
modern: A person who lacks good qualities and has many faults will lose their friends and supporters. This loss of support only strengthens and delights their enemies.

old: There will be no end of lofty delights to the victorious, if their foes are (both) ignorant and timid
modern: The joy of victory is endless when the enemy is both ignorant and timid.

old: The light (of fame) will never be gained by him who gains not the trifling reputation of having fought an unlearned (foe)
modern: Someone who avoids fighting an unlearned person will never gain fame.

old: The evil of hatred is not of a nature to be desired by one even in sport
modern: No one should desire or practice the evil of enmity, not even as a joke or for fun.

old: Though you may incur the hatred of warriors whose ploughs are bows, incur not that of ministers whose ploughs are words
modern: You can make enemies with warriors who use bows, but you should not make enemies with scholars who use words.

old: He who being alone, incurs the hatred of many is more infatuated than even mad men
modern: Someone who is alone and makes many enemies is more foolish than even a mad person.

old: The world abides in the greatness of that good-natured man who behaves so as to turn hatred into friendship.
modern: The world depends on the greatness of a good-natured ruler who turns his enemies into friends. The world remains secure under his capable and powerful rule.

old: He who is alone and helpless while his foes are two should secure one of them as an agreeable help (to himself)
modern: If someone is alone and has no allies against two enemies, they should make one of those enemies a friendly ally.

old: Though (one's foe is) aware or not of one's misfortune one should act so as neither to join nor separate (from him)
modern: Whether you trust your enemy or not, during a time of disaster, you should neither join them nor separate from them.

old: Relate not your suffering even to friends who are ignorant of it, nor refer to your weakness in the presence of your foes
modern: Do not tell your pain to people who are unaware of it, and do not show your weakness to your enemies.

old: The joy of one's foes will be destroyed if one guards oneself by knowing the way (of acting) and securing assistance
modern: By knowing how to act, strengthening yourself, and seeking protection, the pride and joy of your enemies will naturally be destroyed.

old: A thorny tree should be felled while young, (for) when it is grown it will destroy the hand of the feller
modern: You should destroy your enemies when they are weak, because when they become strong, they will destroy you.

old: Those who do not destroy the pride of those who hate (them) will certainly not exist even to breathe
modern: Someone who does not crush the pride of their enemies will not even survive long enough to breathe. Those who fail to destroy the arrogance of those who hate them will surely be killed by their enemies before they can even take a breath.

old: Shade and water are not pleasant, (if) they cause disease; so are the qualities of (one's) relations not agreeable, (if) they cause pain
modern: Water and shade are good only if they don't cause harm, and relatives are good only if they don't cause harm.

old: Fear not foes (who say they would cut) like a sword; (but) fear the friendship of foes (who seemingly
modern: You do not need to fear enemies who are openly hostile like drawn swords, but you should fear the friendship of enemies who pretend to be allies.

old: Fear internal enmity and guard yourself; (if not) it will destroy (you) in an evil hour, as surely as the tool which cuts the potter's clay
modern: One should guard against internal enemies, as they will inevitably destroy you during a time of weakness just like a tool that cuts a potter's clay.

old: The secret enmity of a person whose mind in unreformed will lead to many evils causing disaffection among (one's) relations
modern: If a person harbors secret inner hostility, it causes many evils and makes their own relatives turn against them.

old: If there appears internal hatred in a (king's) family; it will lead to many a fatal crime
modern: If hidden hatred arises among close relatives, it will cause many fatal harms and crimes.

old: If hatred arises among (one's) own people, it will be hardly possible (for one) to escape death
modern: If hatred arises among one's own people, it is always hard to escape death. If discord finds a place among those who lived together in unity, it is ever hard to keep destruction away.

old: Never indeed will a family subject to internal hatred unite (really) though it may present an apparent union like that of a casket and its lid
modern: A family with internal hatred cannot truly unite, even if it appears united on the outside like a lid on a box.

old: A family subject to internal hatred will wear out and lose its strength like iron that has been filed away
modern: A household with internal hatred loses its strength like iron being worn down by a file.

old: Although internal hatred be as small as the fragment of the sesamum (seed), still does destruction dwell in it
modern: Even if internal hatred is as small as a split in a sesame seed, it contains the potential for great destruction.

old: Living with those who do not agree (with one) is like dwelling with a cobra (in the same) hut
modern: Living with people who are not in agreement with you is like dwelling in a hut with a snake.

old: Not to disregard the power of those who can carry out (their wishes) is more important than all the watchfulness of those who guard (themselves against evil)
modern: It is the best protection to not despise the power of those who can successfully complete their actions. This is better than all the other safeguards people use to protect themselves from harm.

old: To behave without respect for the great (rulers) will make them do (us) irremediable evils
modern: If you do not respect powerful people, they will cause you endless suffering.

old: If a person desires ruin, let him not listen to the righteous dictates of law, but commit crimes against those who are able to slay (other sovereigns)
modern: If you want to ruin yourself, do not listen to the advice of the righteous and commit crimes against those who are powerful enough to destroy other kings.

old: The weak doing evil to the strong is like beckoning Yama to come (and destroy them)
modern: When powerless people do evil to those who have power, they are like beckoning Death with their own hands to come and destroy them.

old: Those who have incurred the wrath of a cruel and mighty potentate will not prosper wherever they may go
modern: Someone who has angered a powerful ruler cannot survive anywhere they go.

old: Though burnt by a fire (from a forest), one may perhaps live; (but) never will he live who has shown disrespect to the great (devotees)
modern: Someone who is burned by fire might still survive, but a person who offends the great will not survive.

old: If a king incurs the wrath of the righteous great, what will become of his government with its splendid auxiliaries and (all) its untold wealth ?
modern: If great and worthy people become angry, all the king's wealth and luxurious life are useless.

old: If (the) hill-like (devotees) resolve on destruction, those who seemed to be everlasting will be destroyed root and branch from the earth
modern: If people try to ruin those who are as great as a mountain, even those who seem to be permanently established on earth, along with their families, will be completely destroyed.

old: If those of exalted vows burst in a rage, even (Indra) the king will suffer a sudden loss and be entirely ruined.
modern: If someone of high principles gets angry, even a king will lose his position and be ruined.

old: Though in possession of numerous auxiliaries, they will perish who are-exposed to the wrath of the noble whose penance is boundless
modern: Even someone with massive wealth and powerful allies will not survive if they face the anger of highly virtuous and noble people.

old: Those who lust after their wives will not attain the excellence of virtue; and it is just this that is not desired by those who are bent on acquiring wealth
modern: Someone who is deeply infatuated with their wife and acts exactly as she says will not attain the great benefits of virtue. This kind of pleasure is also rejected by those who are focused on achieving wealth and taking action.

old: The wealth of him who, regardless (of his manliness), devotes himself to his wife's feminine nature will cause great shame (to ali men) and to himself;
modern: A man who abandons his own masculinity to obsessively dote on his wife will bring great shame upon himself and all other men. His wealth will be wasted on her, and he will be left feeling deeply ashamed of his loss of manhood.

old: The frailty that stoops to a wife will always make (her husband) feel ashamed among the good
modern: A man who is submissive to his wife will always feel ashamed when he is among good people.

old: The undertaking of one, who fears his wife and is therefore destitute of (bliss), will never be applauded
modern: A man who fears his wife will not gain salvation, and his actions will not be praised.

old: He that fears his wife will always be afraid of doing good deeds (even) to the good
modern: Someone who fears his wife will always be afraid to do good deeds, even for good people.

old: They that fear the bamboo-like shoulders of their wives will be destitute of manliness though they may flourish like the Gods
modern: Someone who fears their wife's slender arm will have no dignity, even if they live like gods.

old: Even shame faced womanhood is more to be esteemed than the shameless manhood that performs
modern: A woman who has a sense of shame is more honorable than a man who simply obeys her commands.

old: Those who yield to the wishes of their wives will neither relieve the wants of (their) friends nor perform virtuous deeds
modern: Someone who follows their wife's wishes will not help their friends in need or do good deeds.

old: From those who obey the commands of their wives are to be expected neither deeds of virtue, nor those of wealth nor (even) those of pleasure
modern: People who obey their wives' commands will not achieve virtuous deeds, wealth, or pleasure.

old: The foolishness that results from devotion to a wife will never be found in those who possess a reflecting mind and a prosperity (flowing) therefrom
modern: Someone who is intelligent and wealthy will never act foolishly by blindly obeying their wife's orders. People with a strong and thoughtful mind do not fall into the foolishness of being completely devoted to a woman.

old: The sweet words of elegant braceleted (prostitutes) who desire (a man) not from affection but from avarice, will cause sorrow
modern: The sweet words of women who seek a man's wealth rather than his love will ultimately cause him sorrow.

old: One must ascertain the character of the ill-natured women who after ascertaining the wealth (of a man) speak (as if they were) good natured-ones, and avoid intercourse (with them)
modern: Do not associate with women who feign virtue to gain wealth, as they are ill-natured.

old: The false embraces of wealth-loving women are like (hired men) embracing a strange corpse in a dark room
modern: The false embrace of women who only want money is like someone in a dark room hugging a dead body they don't know.

old: The wise who seek the wealth of grace will not desire the base favours of those who regard wealth (and not pleasure) as (their) riches
modern: People who seek the wealth of grace will not desire the low pleasures of prostitutes who only care about money.

old: Those whose knowledge is made excellent by their (natural) sense will not covet the trffling delights
modern: People with excellent, naturally good minds will not desire the cheap physical charms of women who offer their favors to anyone who pays them.

old: Those who would spread (the fame of) their own goodness will not desire the shoulders of those,who rejoice in their accomplishments and bestow their despicable favours (on all who pay)
modern: Wise people who want to spread their good reputation will not associate with women who sell their beauty and talents for money.

old: Those who are destitute of a perfectly (reformed) mind will covet the shoulders of those who embrace (them) while their hearts covet other things
modern: Someone with an unsteady mind will seek the embrace of a woman who is only pretending to love them, because that woman is also thinking of someone else.

old: The wise say that to such as are destitute of discerning sense the embraces of faithless women are (as ruinous as those of) the celestail female
modern: Someone without the ability to discern is lured by the embraces of deceitful women, which are as ruinous as the touch of a celestial enchantress who kills with desire.

old: The delicate shoulders of prostitutes with excellent jewels are a hell into which are plunged the ignorant base
modern: The soft, jewelled arms of prostitutes are a hell into which degraded people fall.

old: Treacherous women, liquor, and gambling are the associates of such as have forsaken by Fortune
modern: Treacherous women, alcohol, and gambling are the companions of people who have been abandoned by the goddess of wealth.

old: Those who always thirst after drink will neither inspire fear (in others) nor retain the light (of their fame)
modern: Someone who is addicted to alcohol will not be feared by their enemies and will lose their fame.

old: Let no liquor be drunk; if it is desired, let it be drunk by those who care not for esteem of the great
modern: Do not drink liquor, but if you must, drink only if you do not care about the esteem of wise people.

old: Intoxication is painful even in the presence of (one's) mother; what will it not then be in that of the wise ?
modern: A drunkard's joy is painful even to his mother's face, so how much worse must it be in the presence of the wise? Even a mother who forgives her son's mistakes cannot bear to see him intoxicated, so how will the truly wise tolerate it?

old: The fair maid of modesty will turn her back on those who are guilty of the great and abominable crime of drunkenness
modern: Good shame turns its back on those who commit the great crime of drinking intoxicating liquor.

old: To give money and purchase unconsciousness is the result of one's ignorance of (one's own actions)
modern: Giving money to buy unconsciousness is a sign of ignorance. It is foolish to spend wealth to lose awareness of oneself.

old: They that sleep resemble the deed; (likewise) they that drink are no other than poison-eaters
modern: People who sleep are just like the dead, and people who drink toddy are just like people who drink poison because they lose their senses.

old: Those who always intoxicate themselves by a private (indulgence in) drink; will have their secrets detected and laughed at by their fellow-townsmen
modern: Someone who secretly drinks alcohol and loses their senses will have their condition discovered by their fellow townspeople, who will laugh at them every day.

old: Let (the drunkard) give up saying "I have never drunk"; (for) the moment (he drinks) he will simply betray his former attempt to conceal
modern: Someone who drinks alcohol should stop claiming they never drink, because any wrongdoing they have hidden in their mind will be revealed the moment they lose their self-control.

old: Reasoning with a drunkard is like going under water with a torch in search of a drowned man
modern: Reasoning with a drunkard is like searching for someone who has drowned underwater with a torch. Just as a torch cannot help find a submerged person, logical arguments cannot reach the mind of someone who is heavily intoxicated.
