old: When (a drunkard) who is sober sees one who is not, it looks as if he remembered not the evil effects of his (own) drink
modern: When a sober person sees a drunkard, they should remember the exhaustion they themselves felt when they were drunk, which would help them stop drinking.

old: Though able to win, let not one desire gambling; (for) even what is won is like a fish swallowing the iron in fish-hook
modern: Even if you can win at gambling, you should not desire it, because what you win is like a fish swallowing the iron of a fishhook.

old: That they may good obtain, and see a prosperous day? Is there indeed a means of livelihood that can bestow happiness on gamblers who gain one and lose a hundred?
modern: Is there any way for gamblers who lose a hundred to gain one to live a prosperous and good life? No, there is not.

old: If the king is incessantly addicted to the rolling dice in the hope of gain, his wealth and the resources thereof will take their departure and fall into other's hands
modern: If a ruler constantly talks about and plays with dice, his wealth and the income from it will go to his enemies.

old: There is nothing else that brings (us) poverty like gambling which causes many a misery and destroys (one's) reputation
modern: There is nothing else that causes poverty like gambling, which creates many miseries and destroys a person's reputation. Gambling brings many sorrows, ruins one's fame, and leads them into extreme poverty.

old: Penniless are those who by reason of their attachment would never forsake gambling, the gamblingplace and the handling (of dice)
modern: Those who refuse to give up gambling, the gambling hall, and the skill of throwing dice will eventually lose all their wealth.

old: Those who are swallowed by the goddess called "gambling" will never have their hunger satisfied, but suffer the pangs of hell in the next world
modern: Those who are trapped by the goddess of gambling will never be satisfied and will suffer from hunger and pain. They will also experience misery in the afterlife.

old: To waste time at the place of gambling will destroy inherited wealth and goodness of character
modern: If someone wastes their time in a gambling den, it will destroy their inherited wealth and good character.

old: Gambling destroys property, teaches falsehood, puts an end to benevolence, and brings in misery (here and hereafter)
modern: Gambling destroys wealth, leads to falsehood, and removes grace, causing misery.

old: The habit of gambling prevents the attainment of these five: clothing, wealth, food, fame and learning
modern: If a person gambles, they will lose clothing, wealth, food, fame, and learning. These five things will abandon the person who gambles and set their heart on it.

old: As the gambler loves (his vice) the more he loses by it, so does the soul love (the body) the more it suffers through it
modern: As a gambler loves the game more the more he loses, the soul loves the body more the more it suffers.

old: If (food and work are either) excessive or deficient, the three things enumerated by (medical) writers, flatulence, biliousness, and phlegm, will cause (one) disease
modern: If food and work are either excessive or deficient, the three things medical writers count—wind, bile, and phlegm—will cause disease.

old: No medicine is necessary for him who eats after assuring (himself) that what he has (already) eaten has been digested
modern: If you eat only after your previous meal has fully digested, you will not need any medicine for your body.

old: If (one's food has been) digested let one eat with moderation; (for) that is the way to prolong the life of an embodied soul
modern: Eat only after your previous meal has digested, and consume food in the right measure to prolong the life of your body.

old: (First) assure yourself that your food has been digested and never fail to eat, when very hungry, whatever is not disagreeable (to you)
modern: Know that your previous meal has been digested, and when you are very hungry, eat foods that do not change or disagree with your body.

old: There will be no disaster to one's life if one eats with moderation, food that is not disagreeable
modern: If you eat a simple, consistent meal in moderation, you will not suffer from illness.

old: As pleasure dwells with him who eats moderately, so disease (dwells) with the glutton who eats voraciously
modern: Someone who eats moderately experiences lasting pleasure, while a glutton who eats too much suffers from constant illness.

old: He will be afflicted with numberless diseases, who eats immoderately, ignorant (of the rules of health)
modern: If someone eats without measuring their hunger and without considering the size of their stomach, they will suffer from countless diseases.

old: Let the physician enquire into the (nature of the) disease, its cause and its method of cure and treat it faithfully according to (medical rule)
modern: A doctor should first identify the disease, then find its cause, and finally determine the cure, and then treat it without making a mistake. This applies to both physical and social illnesses.

old: The learned (physician) should ascertain the condition of his patient; the nature of his disease, and the season (of the year) and (then) proceed (with his treatment)
modern: A skilled doctor should consider the patient's condition, the nature of the disease, and the season before treating them.

old: Medical science consists of four parts, viz, patient, physician, medicine and compounder; and each of these (again) contains four sub-divisions
modern: Medical treatment involves four things: the patient, the doctor, the medicine, and the person who administers it. Each of these four has its own four sub-categories.

old: Consistency (of thought, word and deed) and fear (of sin) are conjointly natural only to the high-born
modern: Consistency in thought, word, and deed, and a sense of shame, are natural only to those born into a noble family.

old: The high-born will never deviate from these three; good manners, truthfulness and modesty
modern: People of noble birth do not lack good conduct, truth, and modesty. They naturally follow these three qualities without deviation.

old: A cheerful countenance, liberality, pleasant words, and an unreviling disposition, these four are said to be the proper qualities of the truly high-born
modern: A cheerful face, giving what you have, speaking kindly, and not insulting others are the four qualities of a truly noble person.

old: Though blessed with immense wealth, the noble will never do anything unbecoming
modern: Even if they receive billions of wealth, people born into a noble family will not commit actions that degrade their family's honor.

old: Though their means fall off, those born in ancient families, will not lose their character (for liberality)
modern: Even if a person from an ancient family becomes poor, they will not lose their habit of giving.

old: Those who seek to preserve the irreproachable honour of their families will not viciously do what is detrimental thereto
modern: Someone who lives to preserve their family's spotless honor will not stoop to deceitful acts, even in poverty.

old: The defects of the noble will be observed as clearly as the dark spots in the moon.
modern: The faults of a person from a noble family are seen as clearly as the dark spots on the moon.

old: If one of a good family betrays want of affection, his descent from it will be called in question
modern: If someone from a good family shows a lack of affection, people will doubt their ancestry.

old: As the sprout indicates the nature of the soil, (so) the speech of the noble indicates (that of one's birth)
modern: The nature of the soil is shown by the plants that grow from it, and the nature of a person's family is shown by the words they speak.

old: He who desires a good name must desire modesty; and he who desires (the continuance of) a family greatness must be submissive to all
modern: If someone wants to gain a good reputation, they must have modesty, and if they want their family to be respected, they must be humble to everyone.

old: Actions that would degrade (one's) family should not be done; though they may be so important that not doing them would end in death
modern: Even if an action is essential for your life, you should not do anything that would bring shame to your family.

old: Those who desire (to maintain their) honour, will surely do nothing dishonourable, even for the sake of fame
modern: Someone who wants to maintain their honour will not do anything dishonourable, even if it brings them fame.

old: In great prosperity humility is becoming; dignity, in great adversity
modern: In times of great prosperity, one should be humble, and in times of great adversity, one should maintain one's dignity.

old: They who have fallen from their (high) position are like the hair which has fallen from the head
modern: People who fall from their high status are like hair that has fallen from a head. When people of noble birth lose their high position and dignity, they are considered as worthless as hair that has dropped from the head.

old: Even those who are exalted like a hill will be thought low, if they commit deeds that are debasing
modern: Even people who are as great as a mountain will be brought down if they do even a tiny, shameful act.

old: Of what good is it (for the high-born) to go and stand in vain before those who revile him ? it only brings him loss of honour and exclusion from heaven.
modern: Bowing down to people who insult you and losing your self-respect brings no fame in this world and does not lead you to heaven, so what is the use of doing it?

old: It is better for a man to be said of him that he died in his usual state than that he eked out his life by following those who disgraced him
modern: It is better to be said to have died than to live by following those who disrespect you.

old: For the high-born to keep their body in life when their honour is gone will certainly not prove a remedy against death
modern: When a person of high birth loses their honour, a life that only preserves the body is not a cure for death.

old: Those who give up (their) life when (their) honour is at stake are like the yark which kills itself at the loss of (even one of) its hairs
modern: Like a yak that dies if it loses its hair, a person of honour will give up their life if their honour is lost.

old: The world will (always) praise and adore the fame of the honourable who would rather die than suffer indignity
modern: The world will forever praise and honor the memory of honorable people who choose to die rather than live with a ruined reputation.

old: One's light is the abundance of one's courage; one's darkness is the desire to live destitute of such (a state of mind.)
modern: A person's light is their courage to do great things, and their darkness is the thought of living without that courage.

old: All human beings agree as regards their birth but differ as regards their characteristics, because of the different qualities of their actions
modern: All beings are the same in birth, but their work determines their different levels of worth.

old: Though (raised) above, the base cannot become great; though (brought) low, the great cannot become base
modern: Someone who is in a high position but lacks noble qualities is not truly high, and someone who is in a low position but lacks base qualities is not truly low.

old: Even greatness, like a woman's chastity, belongs only to him who guards himself.
modern: Greatness belongs only to someone who guards themselves from straying, just like a faithful woman guards her chastity.

old: (Though reduced) the great will be able to perform, in the proper way, deeds difficult (for others to do)
modern: People with true greatness do difficult deeds in the proper way, even when they face hardships. True greatness is the absence of arrogance or pride, and it is shown by doing rare and difficult actions in the right manner.

old: It is never in the nature of the base to seek the society of the great and partake of their nature
modern: Small-minded people do not have the desire to seek out, befriend, and learn from great people. They do not think about honoring the great and adopting their ways to elevate themselves.

old: Even nobility of birth, wealth and learning, if in (the possession of) the base, will (only) produce everincreasing pride
modern: When people who lack good character gain high status, wealth, or education, they naturally act with extreme arrogance.

old: The great will always humble himself; but the mean will exalt himself in self-admiration
modern: Great people always remain humble, while petty people constantly admire and praise themselves.

old: Freedom from conceit is (the nature of true) greatness; (while) obstinacy therein is (that of) meanness
modern: True greatness is living without arrogance even when there is a reason to be proud, while meanness is swelling with vanity and stopping at the very edge of arrogance.

old: The great hide the faults of others; the base only divulge them
modern: Great people hide the faults of others, while small people only point out their faults.

old: It is said that those who are conscious of their duty and behave with a perfect goodness will regard as natural all that is good
modern: People say that all good qualities are simply a natural duty to those who recognize their responsibilities and live a virtuous life.

old: The only delight of the perfect is that of their goodness; all other (sensual) delights are not to be included among any (true) delights
modern: The good of great people is their good character, and no other good is found in any other good. The beauty of wise people is their good character, and all other external beauties are not included in any beauty. Good character is the only beauty of great people, and no other beauty is a beauty.

old: Affection, fear (of sin), benevolence, favour and truthfulness; these are the five pillars on which perfect goodness rests
modern: Love, modesty, benevolence, grace, and truth are the five pillars that support perfect goodness.

old: Penance consists in the goodness that kills not , and perfection in the goodness that tells not others' faults
modern: True penance is not killing, and true virtue is not speaking ill of others.

old: Stooping (to inferiors) is the strength of those who can accomplish (an undertaking); and that is the weapon with which the great avert their foes
modern: The strength of a capable person is their humility, which is the tool great people use to change their enemies.

old: The touch-stone of perfection is to receive a defeat even at the hands of one's inferiors
modern: The test of a person's worth is their ability to accept defeat even from someone they consider inferior.

old: Of what avail is perfect goodness if it cannot do pleasing things even to those who have pained (it) ?
modern: What good is being good if you don't do good things for those who have hurt you?

old: Poverty is no disgrace to one who abounds in good qualities
modern: Poverty is not a disgrace to someone who possesses the strength of good character and virtue.

old: Those who are said to be the shore of the sea of perfection will never change, though ages may change
modern: People of perfect virtue are like the shore of the sea, and they never change even if ages pass.

old: If there is a defect in the character of the perfect, (even) the great world cannot bear (its) burden
modern: If the great people lose their perfect virtue, the world can no longer bear its own weight.

old: If one is easy of access to all, it will be easy for one to obtain the virtue called goodness
modern: If you are easy to approach and talk to, it is easy to learn good character and courtesy.

old: Affectionateness and birth in a good family, these two constitute what is called a proper behaviour to all
modern: Having affection for others and being born into a harmonious family are the two qualities that make up good character.

old: Resemblance of bodies is no resemblance of souls; true resemblance is the resemblance of qualities that attract
modern: People are not truly alike just because their bodies look similar. True likeness comes from having the same good qualities.

old: The world applauds the character of those whose usefulness results from their equity and charity
modern: The world praises the character of those who live justly and usefully, benefiting others and themselves.

old: Reproach is painful to one even in sport; those (therefore) who know the nature of others exhibit (pleasing) qualities even when they are hated
modern: Even in jest, mocking someone is harmful, so wise people who understand human nature maintain good qualities even when they are dealing with enemies.

old: The (way of the) world subsists by contact with the good; if not, it would bury itself in the earth and perish
modern: The world exists because it is supported by people of good character; without them, it would crumble to dust.

old: He who is destitute of (true) human qualities (only) resembles a tree, though he may possess the sharpness of a file
modern: Even if someone has a sharp intellect like a file, they are just like a tree if they lack good human qualities.

old: It is wrong (for the wise) not to exhibit (good) qualities even towards those who bearing no friendship (for them) do only what is hateful
modern: It is shameful for wise people to lack good qualities and behave badly even towards those who show them no friendship and only do hateful things.

old: To those who cannot rejoice, the wide world is buried darkness even in (broad) day light
modern: To someone who lacks good character and cannot mingle with others and rejoice, even the vast world in broad daylight feels like it is in darkness.

old: The great wealth obtained by one who has no goodness will perish like pure milk spoilt by the
modern: Wealth gained by someone without good character is useless, like pure milk that spoils when kept in a dirty container.

old: He who does not enjoy the immense riches he has heaped up in his house, is (to be reckoned as) dead, (for) there is nothing achieved (by him)
modern: Someone who hoards great wealth but never enjoys it is as good as dead, because they have achieved nothing with their riches.

old: He who knows that wealth yields every pleasure and yet is so blind as to lead miserly life will be born a demon
modern: Someone who hoards wealth without giving to others, believing it can solve everything, will be born into a miserable life.

old: A burden to the earth are men bent on the acquisition of riches and not (true) fame
modern: People who only want to gather wealth and do not desire fame are a burden to the earth.

old: What will the miser who is not liked (by any one) regard as his own (in the world to come) ?
modern: What will a wealthy person who is disliked by everyone expect to survive after they die?

old: Those who neither give (to others) nor enjoy (their property) are (truly) destitute, though possessing immense riches
modern: People who do not share their wealth with others and do not enjoy it themselves are truly destitute, even if they possess crores of riches.

old: He who enjoys not (his riches) nor relieves the wants of the worthy is a disease to his wealth
modern: Great wealth is a disease to someone who does not use it for themselves or give it to worthy people.

old: The wealth of him who never bestows anything on the destitute is like a woman of beauty growing old without a husband
modern: The wealth of someone who does not help the poor is like a beautiful woman who grows old alone.

old: The wealth of him who is disliked (by all) is like the fruit-bearing of the etty tree in the midst of a town
modern: The wealth of someone who is disliked by everyone is like a poisonous tree bearing fruit in the middle of a town.

old: Strangers will inherit the riches that have been acquired without regard for friendship, comfort and charity.
modern: Others will take and enjoy the wealth that someone gathers without showing love, without practicing charity, and while only causing themselves suffering.

old: The short-lived poverty of those who are noble and rich is like the clouds becoming poor (for a while)
modern: When rich and generous people experience a brief period of poverty, it is like rain clouds temporarily becoming thin or empty. Even though this short-lived poverty causes them to temporarily stop giving to others, they will eventually become wealthy again and continue to help the world, just as the clouds will eventually rain again.

old: True modesty is the fear of (evil) deeds; all other modesty is (simply) the bashfulness of virtuous maids
modern: True shame is shrinking from doing evil, while other shame is simply the natural bashfulness of beautiful women.

old: Food, clothing and the like are common to all men but modesty is peculiar to the good
modern: Food, clothing, and other basic needs are common to all living beings, but modesty is a special quality of good people.

old: As the body is the abode of the spirit, so the excellence of modesty is the abode of perfection
modern: All living beings reside in a physical body, and similarly, the virtue of modesty is the home of perfection. Just as a spirit cannot function without a body, perfection cannot exist without the feeling of modesty.

old: Is not the modesty ornament of the noble ? Without it, their haughtiness would be a pain (to others)
modern: Shame is a beautiful ornament for people of dignity, and without it, their proud walk looks like a sickness.

old: The world regards as the abode of modesty him who fear his own and other's guilt
modern: The world considers a person to be the home of shame if they feel ashamed for their own wrongdoing and for the wrongdoing of others.

old: The great make modesty their barrier (of defence) and not the wide world
modern: Great people do not desire the wide world without making modesty their protective fence.

old: The modest would rather lose their life for the sake of modesty than lose modesty for the sake of life
modern: Someone who values modesty would rather give up their life than give up their modesty. They would not abandon their modesty to save their life.

old: Virtue is likely to forsake him who shamelessly does what others are ashamed of
modern: Virtue will abandon someone who shamelessly commits acts that other people are ashamed of.

old: Want of manners injures one's family; but want of modesty injures one's character
modern: A lack of good manners ruins one's family lineage, and a complete lack of shame ruins all of a person's goodness and well-being.

old: The actions of those who are without modesty at heart are like those of puppet moved by a string
modern: The actions of people who have no shame in their hearts are like a wooden puppet moved by a string that is made to look alive. These people are not truly alive, just like the wooden puppet.

chapter: The Way of Maintaining the Family
old: There is no higher greatness than that of one saying I will not cease in my effort (to raise my family)
modern: There is no greater greatness than that of someone who resolves to never slacken their hand in doing their duty to their family without stopping their efforts until the task is complete.

chapter: The Way of Maintaining the Family
old: One's family is raised by untiring perseverance in both effort and wise contrivances
modern: A family grows when someone combines persistent effort with deep wisdom.

chapter: The Way of Maintaining the Family
old: The Deity will clothe itself and appear before him who resolves on raising his family
modern: When someone resolves to elevate their family, the divine power will appear and help them by preparing itself for action.

chapter: The Way of Maintaining the Family
old: Those who are prompt in their efforts (to better their family) need no deliberation, such efforts will of themselves succeed
modern: Those who work quickly to improve their family's status will succeed without needing to plan.

chapter: The Way of Maintaining the Family
old: People will eagerly seek the friendship of the prosperous soul who has raised his family without foul means
modern: People will gather around and claim kinship with someone who lives a blameless life and raises their family well.

chapter: The Way of Maintaining the Family
old: A man's true manliness consists in making himself the head and benefactor of his family
modern: A person shows true worth by making themselves the head and the benefactor of their own family.

chapter: The Way of Maintaining the Family
old: Like heroes in the battle-field, the burden (of protection etc.) is borne by those who are the most efficient in a family.
modern: Just as the strongest, most fearless warriors bear the burden of fighting on the battlefield, the strongest and most capable members of a family bear the responsibility of protecting and carrying the burdens of their household.

chapter: The Way of Maintaining the Family
old: As a family suffers by (one's) indolence and false dignity there is to be so season (good or bad) to those who strive to raise their family
modern: There is no specific season for those who work to uplift their family, and if they become lazy while worrying about their pride, their family's greatness will be destroyed. If they hesitate to act out of fear of hardship or wait for the right time, the welfare of the people will be ruined.

chapter: The Way of Maintaining the Family
old: Is it only to suffering that his body is exposed who undertakes to preserve his family from evil ?
modern: Is the body of someone who tries to protect their family from harm a container only for suffering?

chapter: The Way of Maintaining the Family
old: If there are none to prop up and maintain a family (in distress), it will fall at the stroke of the axe of misfortune
modern: A household will fall when misfortune strikes if there is no good person to support it.

old: Agriculture, though laborious, is the most excellent (form of labour); for people, though they go about (in search of various employments), have at last to resort to the farmer
modern: Farming is the most excellent kind of work although it is laborious, because people who go about in search of other employment must in the end turn to the farmer.

old: Agriculturists are (as it were) the linch-pin of the world for they support all other workers who cannot till the soil
modern: Farmers are the linchpin of the world because they support everyone else who cannot farm.

old: They alone live who live by agriculture; all others lead a cringing, dependent life
modern: Those who live by ploughing and eating their own food are the ones who truly live. Everyone else lives by bowing to others and eating what they are given.

old: Patriotic farmers desire to bring all other states under the control of their own king
modern: Farmers who have abundant grain will see the umbrellas of many kings come under their own king's umbrella.

old: Those whose nature is to live by manual labour will never beg but give something to those who beg
modern: Someone who works with their own hands to earn their food will not beg from others, but will give to those who ask.

old: If the farmer's hands are slackened, even the ascetic state will fail
modern: Even ascetics who claim to have given up all worldly desires depend on farmers to survive, so if the farmers stop working, even the ascetics will starve.

old: If the land is dried so as to reduce one ounce of earth to a quarter, it will grow plentifully even without a handful of manure
modern: If you plow the soil until it is reduced to a quarter of its original weight, you can grow abundant crops without using any manure.

old: Manuring is better than ploughing; after weeding, watching is better than watering (it)
modern: Applying manure is better than ploughing, and weeding is better than watering. However, protecting the crop from harm is even better than all of these.

old: If the owner does not (personally) attend to his cultivation, his land will behave like an angry wife and yield him no pleasure
modern: If the owner does not personally attend to his land, it will become like an angry wife and yield no crops.

old: The maiden, Earth, will laugh at the sight of those who plead poverty and lead an idle life
modern: The good earth will laugh to see people sitting idle and complaining that they are poor. The earth provides wealth to those who work, so she mocks those who do nothing and still complain about being poor.

old: There is nothing that afflicts (one) like poverty
modern: Nothing is more painful than poverty, and poverty itself is the most painful thing.

old: When cruel poverty comes on, it deprives one of both the present and future (bliss)
modern: Poverty is a terrible sin that deprives a person of both present and future happiness.

old: Hankering poverty destroys at once the greatness of (one's) ancient descent and (the dignity of one's) speech
modern: The craving that people call poverty destroys a person's ancient lineage and their dignified speech.

old: Even in those of high birth, poverty will produce the fault of uttering mean words
modern: Poverty causes even people from good families to become tired and utter mean words.

old: The misery of poverty brings in its train many (more) miseries
modern: Wanton poverty is a great misery that brings many other miseries with it.

old: The words of the poor are profitless, though they may be sound in thought and clear in expression
modern: Even if a poor person speaks with deep understanding and conveys good, profound thoughts, people will not listen to or value their words, and their speech will ultimately go to waste.

old: He that is reduced to absolute poverty will be regarded as a stranger even by his own mother
modern: A person who is poor and lacks virtue will be treated like a stranger even by his own mother.

old: Is the poverty that almost killed me yesterday, to meet me today too ?
modern: Will the poverty that almost killed me yesterday come to bother me again today?

old: One may sleep in the midst of fire; but by no means in the midst of poverty
modern: Someone can sleep in the middle of a fire, but in poverty, not even a moment of sleep is possible.

old: The destitute poor, who do not renounce their bodies, only consume their neighbour's salt and water
modern: The destitute who do not renounce their lives cause their neighbor's salt and gruel to go to waste.

old: If you meet with those that may be begged of, you may beg; (but) if they withhold (their gift) it is their blame and not yours
modern: If you find someone who can give, you should ask them for help. If they refuse, the blame is theirs, not yours.

old: Even begging may be pleasant, if what is begged for is obtained without grief (to him that begs)
modern: Even begging for something brings joy if the requested items are given without causing any distress.

old: There is even a beauty in standing before and begging of those who are liberal in their gifts and understand their duty (to beggars)
modern: It is beautiful to beg from someone who has a generous heart and understands their duty to give.

old: To beg of such as never think of withholding (their charity) even in their dreams, is in fact the same as giving (it oneself);
modern: Asking for something from someone who never even thinks of refusing in their dreams is just like giving to others.

old: As there are in the world those that give without refusing, there are (also) those that prefer to beg by simply standing before them
modern: Poor people stand before someone and beg because there are people in the world who give without hiding their wealth or saying no. They do this because they know they will be helped, rather than dying from shame.

old: All the evil of begging will be removed at the sight of those who are far from the evil of refusing
modern: If you see someone who does not hide their wealth and is free from the disease of begging, the poverty and suffering of the beggar will completely disappear.

old: Beggars rejoice exceedingly when they behold those who bestow (their alms) with kindness and courtesy
modern: When someone gives without insulting or scorning the receiver, the receiver's heart is filled with joy.

old: If there were no beggars, (the actions done in) the cool wide world would only resemble the movement of a puppet
modern: If there were no beggars, the movement of the cool wide world would be like wooden puppets being moved by a string.

old: What (praise) would there be to givers (of alms) if there were no beggars to ask for and reveive (them)
modern: What glory is there for those who give if there are no people who ask for and receive their help? Without people who ask, there is no one to praise the givers, so the givers do not get any glory.

old: He who begs ought not to be angry (at a refusal); for even the misery of (his own) poverty should be a sufficient reason (for so doing)
modern: Someone who asks for help should not get angry at a refusal, because their own suffering from poverty is proof enough of their need.

old: Not to beg (at all) even from those excellent persons who cheerfully give without refusing, will do immense good
modern: It is billions of times better to not beg, even from excellent people who happily give whatever they have without hiding it.

old: If the Creator of the world has decreed even begging as a means of livelihood, may he too go abegging and perish
modern: If the Creator of the world has made begging a way of life, then he too should wander and perish.

old: There is no greater folly than the boldness with which one seeks to remedy the evils of poverty by begging (rather than by working)
modern: There is nothing harder than the stubbornness of someone who gives up trying to work and instead believes they can end the misery of poverty by begging.

old: Even the whole world cannot sufficiently praise the dignity that would not beg even in the midst of destitution
modern: The dignity of someone who does not beg even when they have no way to live is a greatness that the whole world cannot contain.

old: Even thin gruel is ambrosia to him who has obtained it by labour
modern: Even if the food is just thin gruel made with water, nothing is sweeter than eating what you earned through your own hard work.

old: There is nothing more disgraceful to one's tongue than to use it in begging water even for a cow
modern: There is nothing more shameful for a person's tongue than begging for water even for a thirsty cow.

old: I beseech all beggars and say, "If you need to beg, never beg of those who give unwillingly."
modern: I ask all beggars to never beg from people who hide their wealth. It is better to not ask for anything at all than to receive a reluctant gift.

old: The unsafe raft of begging will split when it strikes on the rock of refusal
modern: The unsafe raft of begging will split when it strikes the rock of refusal.

old: To think of (the evil of) begging is enough to melt one's heart; but to think of refusal is enough to break it
modern: Thinking of the suffering of beggars melts the heart, but thinking of the cruelty of refusing them breaks it completely.

old: Saying "No" to a beggar takes away his life. (but as that very word will kill the refuser) where then would the latter's life hide itself ?
modern: When someone who asks is told "no," they lose their life, so where can the life of the person who denies them hide?

old: The base resemble men perfectly (as regards form); and we have not seen such (exact) resemblance (among any other species)
modern: Bad people look exactly like good people in outward form, but we have never seen any other species that resembles humans so closely. Because they look so much like humans, their bad character is not easily noticed.

old: The low enjoy more felicity than those who know what is good; for the former are not troubled with anxiety (as to the good)
modern: People who lack a sense of right and wrong are considered wealthier because they do not worry about doing good deeds or the consequences of their actions, while those who understand what is good are constantly troubled by anxiety and fear.

old: The base resemble the Gods; for the base act as they like
modern: The base act like the gods because they do whatever they want without any restrictions. They can do whatever they wish because no one controls them.

old: The base feels proud when he sees persons whose acts meaner than his own
modern: When a base person sees someone who acts even lower than they do, they feel superior and become arrogant.

old: (The principle of) behaviour in the mean is chiefly fear; if not, hope of gain, to some extent
modern: The conduct of base people is driven by fear, and if that fails, the hope of gaining what they desire provides a little bit of discipline.

old: The base are like a drum that is beaten, for they unburden to others the secrets they have heard
modern: Base people are like a beaten drum because they spread the secrets they have heard.

old: The mean will not (even) shake off (what sticks to) their hands (soon after a meal) to any but those who would break their jaws with their clenched fists
modern: Someone who is stingy will not shake off the food stuck to their hands for anyone except those who would break their jaws with their clenched fists.

old: The great bestow (their alms) as soon as they are informed; (but) the mean, like the sugar-cane, only when they are tortured to death
modern: Good people give to you as soon as you tell them your problems, but bad people only give when you pressure and torture them like crushing sugarcane.

old: The base will bring an evil (accusation) against others, as soon as he sees them (enjoying) good food
modern: When a lowly person sees others wearing nice clothes and eating good food, they become jealous and will deliberately look for faults to accuse them of.

old: The base will hasten to sell themselves as soon as a calamity has befallen them. For what else are they fitted ?
modern: When a calamity strikes, a base person will quickly sell themselves. They are fit for nothing else.

old: Is this jewelled female a celestial, a choice peahen, or a human being ? My mind is perplexed
modern: Is the woman wearing heavy earrings a goddess, a beautiful peacock, or a human woman? My mind is completely bewildered trying to figure out who she is.

old: This female beauty returning my looks is like a celestial maiden coming with an army to contend against me
modern: When the beautiful woman returned my gaze, her counter glance felt like a weaponized arrow bringing an army to attack me. Her looking back at me felt like a striking force bringing troops to fight me.

old: I never knew before what is called Yama; I see it now; it is the eyes that carry on a great fight with (the help of) female qualities
modern: I never knew what was called death before, but I understand it now; it is the large, fighting eyes that carry the qualities of a woman.

old: These eyes that seem to kill those who look at them are as it were in hostilities with this feminine simplicity
modern: The woman's simple and feminine appearance is contradicted by her eyes, which seem to drink the life of anyone who looks at them.

old: Is it Yama, (a pair of) eyes or a hind ?- Are not all these three in the looks of this maid ?
modern: Is the young woman's gaze a deadly weapon, a darting eye, or a frightened deer? It possesses all three qualities.

old: Her eyes will cause (me) no trembling sorrow, if they are properly hidden by her cruel arched eyebrows
modern: If her cruel, arched eyebrows were to hide her eyes, they would not cause me the sorrow that makes me tremble.

old: The cloth that covers the firm bosom of this maiden is (like) that which covers the eyes of a rutting elephant
modern: A piece of cloth draped over a woman's firm breasts is like a cloth placed over the eyes of a rutting elephant.

old: On her bright brow alone is destroyed even that power of mine that used to terrify the most fearless
modern: My power that once terrified my enemies in battle has been destroyed by the sight of my beloved's beautiful brow.

old: Of what use are other jewels to her who is adorned with modesty, and the meek looks of a hind ?
modern: What use are other jewels to a woman who is already adorned with the meek looks of a fawn and modesty?

old: Unlike boiled honey which yields delight only when it is drunk, love gives pleasure even when looked at
modern: Unlike wine which only gives pleasure when drunk, love gives pleasure just by being seen.

old: There are two looks in the dyed eyes of this (fair one); one causes pain, and the other is the cure thereof
modern: Her painted eyes have two kinds of glances, one that causes pain and the other that cures that pain.

old: A single stolen glance of her eyes is more than half the pleasure (of sexual embrace)
modern: A stolen, furtive glance from her eyes is greater than half the pleasure of sexual embrace.

old: She has looked (at men) and stooped (her head); and that (sign) waters as it were (the corn of) our love
modern: She looked at him and, out of shyness, bowed her head, which was like watering the growing crop of love between them.

old: When I look, she looks down; when I do not, she looks and smiles gently
modern: When I look at her, she looks down at the ground, but when I look away, she looks at me and smiles gently.

old: She not only avoids a direct look at me, but looks as it were with a half-closed eye and smiles
modern: She does not look directly at me, but instead looks with one eye half-closed as if smiling to herself.

old: Though they may speak harshly as if they were strangers, the words of the friendly are soon understood
modern: Even if someone speaks harsh words like a stranger, you will quickly understand that they are actually friendly and hold no hatred in their heart.

old: Little words that are harsh and looks that are hateful are (but) the expressions of lovers who wish to act like strangers
modern: Even if someone speaks harsh words without any anger and looks at you like an enemy, they are actually showing signs of their love. They are just pretending to be strangers on the outside while caring deeply on the inside.

old: When I look, the pitying maid looks in return and smiles gently; and that is a comforting sign for me
modern: When I look at her, the tender maid smiles gently, and that soft smile brings a comforting beauty to her swaying form.

old: Both the lovers are capable of looking at each other in an ordinary way, as if they were perfect strangers
modern: Lovers have the natural habit of looking at each other in public as if they were complete strangers. They act as though they do not know each other, even though they secretly feel a deep, joyful love.

old: The words of the mouths are of no use whatever, when there is perfect agreement between the eyes (of lovers)
modern: When two people in love look into each other's eyes, words are useless.

old: The (simultaneous) enjoyment of the five senses of sight, hearing, taste, smell and touch can only be found with bright braceleted (women)
modern: All the pleasures of the five senses—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—can be fully experienced at the same time with a woman wearing shining bangles.

old: The remedy for a disease is always something different (from it); but for the disease caused by this jewelled maid, she is herself the cure
modern: The cure for a disease is something different from it, but for the disease caused by this woman, she herself is the cure.

old: Can the lotus-eyed Vishnu's heaven be indeed as sweet to those who delight to sleep in the delicate arms of their beloved ?
modern: Is the lotus-eyed lord's heaven as sweet as sleeping in the soft arms of a beloved?

old: From whence has she got this fire that burns when I withdraw and cools when I approach ?
modern: The woman has a fire in her that burns when I move away and cools when I get close. Where did she get this unique fire to put it in my heart?

old: The shoulders of her whose locks are adorned with flowers delight me as if they were the very sweets I have desired (to get).
modern: The shoulders of the woman with flower-adorned hair bring me joy just like the exact things I desired when I first wished for them.

old: The shoulders of this fair one are made of ambrosia, for they revive me with pleasure every time I embrace them
modern: The simple maiden's shoulders are made of ambrosia, and when I embrace her, my withered life puts forth its buds again.

old: The embraces of a gold-complexioned beautiful female are as pleasant as to dwell in one's own house and live by one's own (earnings) after distributing (a portion of it in charity)
modern: Embracing a beautiful, dark-complexioned woman is as pleasant as staying at home and enjoying the food you earned and shared with others.

old: To ardent lovers sweet is the embrace that cannot be penetrated even by a breath of breeze
modern: A tight embrace where not even a breath of air can pass between two loving partners is sweet.

old: Love quarrel, reconciliation and intercourse - these are the advantages reaped by those who marry for lust
modern: Married people gain the benefits of love through the joys of a lover's tryst: a lover's quarrel, reconciling after realizing the mistake, and reuniting.

old: As (one's) ignorance is discovered the more one learns, so does repeated intercourse with a welladorned female (only create a desire for more)
modern: As people learn more and discover their past ignorance, repeated intimacy with a beautifully adorned woman only creates an endless desire for more.

old: May you flourish, O Anicham! you have a delicate nature But my beloved is more delicate than you
modern: O anicham flower, may you flourish, for you have a very delicate nature, but my beloved is even more delicate than you.

old: O my soul, fancying that flowers which are seen by many can resemble her eyes, you become confused at the sight of them
modern: My heart, you become confused when you see flowers, thinking they resemble her eyes, which many people get to see.

old: The complexion of this bamboo-shouldered one is that of a shoot; her teeth, are pearls; her breath,
modern: She has a body like a tender shoot, teeth like pearls, breath like a fragrant scent, and eyes like a sharp spear, all with shoulders like bamboo.

old: If the blue lotus could see, it would stoop and look at the ground saying, "I can never resemble the eyes of this excellent jewelled one."
modern: If the lilies could see the woman with the beautiful jeweled eyes, they would bow their heads and look at the ground in shame because they could never match her eyes.

old: No merry drums will be beaten for the (tender) waist of her who has adorned herself with the anicham without having removed its stem
modern: If a woman wears anicham flowers without removing their stems, her delicate waist will be pained and no auspicious drums will be beaten for her.

old: The stars have become confused in their places not being able to distinguish between the moon and the maid's countenance
modern: The stars are confused and moving wildly because they cannot tell the difference between the moon and the woman's face.

old: Could there be spots in the face of this maid like those in the bright full moon ?
modern: Does this woman's face have any blemishes, just like the phases of the waxing and waning moon?

old: If you can indeed shine like the face of women, flourish, O moon, for then would you be worth loving ?
modern: If you could shine like a woman's face, you would be worthy of my love.

old: O moon, if you wish to resemble the face of her whose eyes are like (these) flowers, do not appear so as to be seen by all
modern: Moon, if you want to look like the face of the woman with flower-like eyes, then do not appear where many people can see you.

old: The anicham and the feathers of the swan are to the feet of females, like the fruit of the (thorny) Nerunji
modern: The soft anicham flower and the swan's down are painful to the delicate feet of women, just like the thorny nerunji fruit.

old: The water which oozes from the white teeth of this soft speeched damsel is like a mixture of milk and honey
modern: The water oozing from the white teeth of the soft-spoken woman is as sweet as milk mixed with honey.

old: The love between me and this damsel is like the union of body and soul
modern: The love between me and this woman is exactly like the bond between the soul and the body. The soul and the body cannot be separated from each other, and we are just as inseparable.

old: O you image in the pupil (of my eye)! depart; there is no room for (my) fair-browed beloved
modern: O image in my pupil, leave because there is no room for my beautiful-browed beloved.

old: My fair-jewelled one resembles the living soul (when she is in union with me), the dying soul when she leaves me
modern: When the woman adorned with fine ornaments is with me, she is like life to my soul; when she leaves me, she is like death to my soul.

old: If I had forgotten her who has bright battling eyes, I would have remembered (thee); but I never forget her (Thus says he to her maid)
modern: If I could forget the qualities of the woman with bright, battling eyes, I would remember you; but I never forget her, so I do not remember you.

old: My lover would not depart from mine eyes; even if I wink, he would not suffer (from pain); he is so ethereal
modern: My lover's subtle form never leaves my eyes, and he does not mind even if I blink.

old: As my lover abides in my eyes, I will not even paint them, for he would (then) have to conceal himself
modern: Because my lover lives inside my eyes, I do not paint them with kohl, knowing that he would have to hide if I did.

old: As my lover is in my heart, I am afraid of eating (anything) hot, for I know it would pain him
modern: My lover lives in my heart, so I am afraid to eat hot food because I don't want it to burn him.

old: I will not wink, knowing that if I did, my lover would hide himself; and for this reason, this town says, he is unloving
modern: The speaker keeps their eyes open so their lover hiding inside them does not disappear, because the townspeople will call him unloving.

old: My lover dwells in my heart with perpetual delight; but the town says he is unloving and (therefore) dwells afar
modern: My lover is always happy inside my heart, but the people of the town, not knowing this, say he is unloving and lives far away.

old: To those who after enjoyment of sexual pleasure suffer (for want of more), there is no help so efficient as the palmyra horse
modern: For those who suffer from unfulfilled passion, there is no help as effective as the palmyra horse.

old: Having got rid of shame, the suffering body and soul save themselves on the palmyra horse
modern: My body and soul, unable to bear the pain of separation, have decided to abandon shame and ride the palmyra horse.

old: Modesty and manliness were once my own; now, my own is the palmyra horse that is ridden by the lustful
modern: I once possessed modesty and true manliness, but today I only have the palmyra horse ridden by lustful people.

old: The raft of modesty and manliness, is, alas, carried-off by the strong current of lust
modern: The strong current of lust sweeps away the raft of shame and good manliness.

old: She with the small garland-like bracelets has given me the palmyra horse and the sorrow that is endured at night
modern: The girl with the small, garland-like bracelets gave me the palmyra horse and the sorrow I feel at night.

old: Mine eyes will not close in sleep on your mistress's account; even at midnight will I think of mounting the palmyra horse
modern: My eyes won't sleep because of my beloved, so I will think of climbing the palmyra tree even at midnight.

old: There is nothing so noble as the womanly nature that would not ride the palmyra horse, though plunged a sea of lust
modern: There is no birth as noble as a woman who, though suffering from a sea-like lust, does not ride the palmyra horse.

old: Even the Lust (of women) transgresses its secrecy and appears in public, forgetting that they are too chaste and liberal (to be overcome by it)
modern: Lust betrays its secrecy and becomes public, without considering that the woman is highly soft, chaste, and worthy of pity.

old: My lust, feeling that it is not known by all, reels confused in the streets (of this town).
modern: My love, thinking no one knows it, wanders confusedly in the streets.

old: Even strangers laugh (at us) so as to be seen by us, for they have not suffered
modern: Fools laugh at me to my face because they have never experienced the pain I have suffered.

old: My precious life is saved by the raise of rumour, and this, to my good luck no others are aware of
modern: My life is sustained because the rumor of our love is spreading, and to my good luck, most people do not know the real reason behind it.

old: Not knowing the value of her whose eyes are like flowers this town has got up a rumour about me
modern: The town, not knowing the value of the woman with flower-like eyes, spread a rumor about me, which helped me.

old: Will I not get a rumour that is known to the (whole) town ? For what I have not got is as if I had got it (already)
modern: Hearing the town talk about my love is a gain for me, as if I have already obtained what I have not yet gotten.

old: Rumour increases the violence of my passion; without it it would grow weak and waste away
modern: The rumor circulating in town fuels my passion, and without it, my love would lose its vitality and fade away.

old: As drinking liquor is delightful (to one) whenever one is in mirth, so is lust delightful to me whenever it is the subject of rumour
modern: As drinking liquor becomes more delightful the more one drinks, lust becomes more delightful the more it is talked about.

old: It was but a single day that I looked on (my lover); but the rumour thereof has spread like the seizure of the moon by the serpent
modern: I saw my lover for only a single day, but the resulting rumors spread throughout the world like a snake swallowing the moon.

old: This malady (of lust) is manured by the talk of women and watered by the (harsh) words of my mother
modern: The town's gossip acts as manure, and my mother's harsh words act as water, making this love-sickness grow. The town's gossip provides the fertilizer, and my mother's scolding provides the water for this love-sickness to grow.

old: To say that one could extinguish passion by rumour is like extinguishing fire with ghee
modern: Trying to stop passion with gossip is like trying to put out a fire with ghee.

old: When the departure of him who said "fear not" has put me to shame before others, why need I be ashamed of scandal
modern: When the one who told me not to fear has left me, causing others to feel shame, why should I be ashamed of the rumors they are spreading?

old: The rumour I desire is raised by the town (itself); and my lover would if desired consent (to my following him)
modern: The town is spreading the rumor I want, so my lover will now grant my wish.

old: If it is not departure, tell me; but if it is your speedy return, tell it to those who would be alive then
modern: If you are not leaving, tell me. If you are returning quickly, tell those who will be alive then.

old: His very look was once pleasing; but (now) even intercourse is painful through fear of separation
modern: His very presence was once a source of joy, but now even being close to him is painful because of the fear of separation.

old: As even the lover who understands (everything) may at times depart, confidence is hardly possible
modern: It is hard to trust someone who understands you, because even a knowledgeable lover may eventually leave.

old: If he who bestowed his love and said "fear not" should depart, will it be the fault of those who believed in (his) assuring words ?
modern: If the one who said "fear not" and gave his love should depart, is there any fault for those who trusted his clear words?

old: If you would save (my life), delay the departure of my destined (husband); for if he departs, intercourse will become impossible
modern: If you want to save my life, you must prevent my destined husband from leaving, because if he departs, it will be difficult for us to meet again.

old: If he is so cruel as to mention his departure (to me), the hope that he would bestow (his love) must be given up.
modern: If someone is cruel enough to say they are leaving, it is pointless to hope they will return and show love.

old: Do not the rings that begin to slide down my fingers forebode the separation of my lord ?
modern: The bangles slipping from my hand are announcing that my lord is leaving.

old: Painful is it to live in a friendless town; but far more painful is it to part from one's lover
modern: Living in a town where there are no friends is painful, but parting from a beloved lover is even more painful.

old: Fire burns when touched; but, like the sickness of love, can it also burn when removed ?
modern: Fire burns when touched, but love's sickness burns even when people are apart.

old: As if there were many indeed that can consent to the impossible, kill their pain, endure separation and yet continue to live afterwards
modern: Many people can endure the pain of separation and continue to live, but I cannot.

old: I would hide this pain from others; but it (only) swells like a spring to those who drain it
modern: I want to hide my love sickness from others, but it only swells like a spring to those who draw water from it. The more I try to conceal my suffering, the more it grows.

old: I cannot conceal this pain, nor can I relate it without shame to him who has caused it
modern: I cannot hide this love sickness, nor can I bring myself to tell the person who caused it.

old: (Both) lust and shame, with my soul for their shoulder pole balance themselves on a body that cannot bear them
modern: My soul acts as a pole, and on either end of it, lust and shame hang like burdens on my body, which cannot bear their weight.

old: There is indeed a flood of lust; but there is no raft of safety to cross it with
modern: There is a sea of lust, but there is no raft to cross it safely. This is a sea of the pain of love, and there is no safe boat to swim across it.

old: He who can produce sorrow from friendship, what can he not bring forth out of enmity ?.
modern: Someone who causes sorrow even in friendship, what can they not do when they become enemies?

old: The pleasure of lust is (as great as) the sea; but the pain of lust is far greater
modern: The pleasure of love is like the sea, but the pain of love is even greater.

old: I have swam across the terrible flood of lust, but have not seen its shore; even at midnight I am alone; still I live
modern: I swim the fierce waves of love but cannot see its shore, and I am alone even in the middle of the night.

old: The night which graciously lulls to sleep all living creatures, has me alone for her companion
modern: The night lulls all living creatures to sleep, leaving me alone without any companion.

old: The long nights of these days are far more cruel than the heartless one who is torturing me
modern: The long, slow nights of these days are even crueler than the cruelty of the cruel person who is torturing me.

old: Could mine eyes travel like my thoughts to the abode (of my absent lord), they would not swim in this flood of tears
modern: If my eyes could travel to my lover just like my mind, they would not have to swim in this flood of tears.

old: As this incurable malady has been caused by my eyes which showed (him) to me, why should they now weep for (him)
modern: The incurable disease of love happened because my eyes showed me the lover, so why are those same eyes crying and asking me to show him to them today?

old: The dyed eyes that (then) looked without foresight, why should they now endure sorrow, without feeling sharply (their own fault)
modern: The eyes that looked without understanding the consequences back then are now suffering in sorrow without realizing that they brought this upon themselves.

old: They themselves looked eagerly (on him) and now they weep. Is not this to be laughed at ?
modern: The eyes eagerly looked at her lover on that day, but today they weep on their own, which is a laughable sight.

old: These painted eyes have caused me a lasting mortal disease; and now they can weep no more, the tears having dried up
modern: These painted eyes have given me an incurable, inescapable love disease and then stopped weeping, drying up from their own tears.

old: Mine eyes have caused me a lust that is greater than the sea and (they themselves) endure the torture of sleeplessness
modern: My eyes caused a lust greater than the sea, and now they suffer sleeplessly from that same pain.

old: The eyes that have given me this disease have themselves been seized with this (suffering) Oh! I am much delighted
modern: The eyes that caused my love-sickness have themselves fallen into the same suffering, and I find this very sweet. It feels like a relief to see them weep sleeplessly, suffering just as I do.

old: The eyes that became tender and gazed intently on him, may they suffer so much as to dry up the fountain of their tears
modern: The eyes that once gazed with such tender longing at the lover they desired should suffer through sleepless nights of sorrow today, until all their tears completely dry up.

old: He is indeed here who loved me with his lips but not with his heart but mine eyes suffer from not seeing him
modern: There is someone here who loved me with his words but not with his heart, and my eyes cannot find peace without seeing him.

old: When he is away they do not sleep; when he is present they do not sleep; in either case, mine eyes endure unbearable agony
modern: The eyes of someone in love do not sleep when their lover is away, and they do not sleep when the lover is present. In both situations, the eyes endure unbearable agony.

old: It is not difficult for the people of this place to understand the secret of those whose eyes, like mine, are as it were beaten drums
modern: It is not hard for the people of this town to know a secret when someone has eyes like mine that reveal what is hidden in the heart.

old: I who (then) consented to the absence of my loving lord, to whom can I (now) relate the fact of my having turned sallow
modern: I consented to my lover's absence, so now that I have turned pale from the pain of missing him, who can I tell about my fading complexion?

old: Sallowness, as if proud of having been caused by him, would now ride on my person
modern: The paleness on my body creeps and spreads, proudly claiming that the lover created it.

old: He has taken (away) my beauty and modesty, and given me instead disease and sallowness
modern: He took my beauty and modesty and left me with disease and a pale complexion.

old: I think (of him); and what I speak about is but his excellence; still is there sallowness; and this is deceitful
modern: I think of his words and speak of his excellence, yet this pallor has come, which is deceitful.

old: Just as my lover departed then, did not sallowness spread here on my person ?
modern: My lover left, and my body grew pale.

old: Just as darkness waits for the failing light; so does sallowness wait for the laxity of my husband's intercourse
modern: Just as darkness waits for a lamp to fade, a woman's pallor waits for her lover's embrace to weaken. This fading happens when his tight embrace slightly loosens, and it might also happen if they are separated.

old: I who was in close embrace just turned aside and the moment I did so, sallowness came on me like something to be seized on
modern: While I was lying in my lover's embrace, I unknowingly shifted a little to the side, and at that very moment, a paleness spread over me as if it were being scooped up.

old: Besides those who say "she has turned sallow" there are none who say "he has forsaken her"
modern: People blame her for becoming pale, but no one says that he is the one who left her.

old: If he is clear of guilt who has conciliated me (to his departure) let my body suffer its due and turn sallow
modern: If the person who convinced me to accept this separation is truly well, then my body should turn pale.

old: It would be good to be said of me that I have turned sallow, if friends do not reproach with unkindness him who pleased me (then)
modern: It is good to be called pale if people do not insult the lover who made me agree to our separation by withholding his affection.

old: The women who are beloved by those whom they love, have they have not got the stone-less fruit of sexual delight ?
modern: Someone who is loved by the person they love has obtained the stoneless fruit of love.

old: The bestowal of love by the beloved on those who love them is like the rain raining (at the proper season) on those who live by it
modern: The love that a beloved shows to someone who loves them is like the rain that falls on living beings.

old: The pride that says "we shall live" suits only those who are loved by their beloved (husbands)
modern: The pride of living belongs only to those who are loved in return by the one they love.

old: Even those who are esteemed (by other women) are devoid of excellence, if they are not loved by their beloved
modern: Even if someone is highly respected by society, they are considered unlucky and lacking in goodness if they are not loved by the person they love. If a woman is not loved by the husband she desires, she is considered unfortunate.

old: He who is beloved by me, what will he do to me, if I am not beloved by him ?
modern: What good can someone who does not love us in return do for us?

old: Lust, like the weight of the KAVADI, pains if it lies in one end only but pleases if it is in both
modern: It is painful if love is felt by only one person, but it is pleasant when both sides feel it equally, just like a balanced load on a carrying pole.

old: Would not cupid who abides and contends in one party (only) witness the pain and sorrow (in that party)?
modern: The god of love, who only acts on one side, does not see the pain and sorrow caused by the change in my complexion.

old: There is no one in the world so hard-hearted as those who can live without receiving (even) a kind word from their beloved
modern: There is no one in the world as hard-hearted as someone who lives without receiving a single kind word from the person they love.

old: Though my beloved bestows no love on one, still are his words sweet to my ears
modern: Even though the man I love does not return my affection, any word spoken about him is sweet to my ears.

old: Live, O my soul, would you who relate your great sorrow to strangers, try rather to fill up your own sea (of sorrow)
modern: My heart, live on! You are telling your deep sorrow to people who do not love you. Instead, try to empty the sea that is causing you this sorrow, because that is an easier task.

old: Sexuality is sweeter than liquor, because when remembered, it creates a most rapturous delight
modern: Love is sweeter than wine because thinking about past intimacy creates an endless, rapturous delight. Even when separated, simply remembering the joy of being together brings a happiness that outlasts the temporary pleasure of drinking liquor.

old: Even to think of one's beloved gives one no pain Sexuality, in any degree, is always delightful
modern: Thinking of one's beloved removes the pain of separation, so love is always sweet.

old: I feel as if I am going to sneeze but do not, and (therefore) my beloved is about to think (of me) but does not
modern: I feel like I'm about to sneeze but it doesn't happen, and I feel like my lover is about to think of me but he doesn't.

old: He continues to abide in my soul, do I likewise abide in his ?
modern: He is always in my heart, so am I always in his heart?

old: He who has imprisoned me in his soul, is he ashamed to enter incessantly into mine
modern: Someone who keeps me out of his heart is not ashamed to keep entering my heart.

old: I live by remembering my (former) intercourse with him; if it were not so, how could I live ?
modern: I am still alive only because I remember the happy days I spent with him. If I did not have those memories, how could I possibly stay alive?

old: I have never forgotten (the pleasure); even to think of it burns my soul; could I live, if I should ever forget it ?
modern: Even when I try to forget my lover, the pain of separation burns my heart; what will happen to me if I actually manage to forget?

old: He will not be angry however much I may think of him; is it not so much the delight my beloved
modern: Even if I think of him constantly, my beloved will not get angry, and isn't this the great favor he does for me?

old: My precious life is wasting away by thinking too much on the cruelty of him who said we were not different
modern: My life is fading away because I keep thinking about the cruelty of the person who used to say we were one and the same.

old: May you live, O Moon! Do not set, that I mine see him who has departed without quitting my soul
modern: O Moon, live on and do not set so that I can see with my eyes the one who left me but never left my mind.

old: Where with shall I feast the dream which has brought me my dear one's messenger ?
modern: How shall I host a feast for the dream that brought my beloved's messenger?

old: If my fish-like painted eyes should, at my begging, close in sleep, I could fully relate my sufferings to my lord
modern: If my fish-like eyes close in sleep as I beg, I will tell my lover in a dream about the life I have survived.

old: My life lasts because in my dream I behold him who does not favour me in my waking hours
modern: My life continues because I see in my dreams the one who does not show me kindness when I am awake.

old: There is pleasure in my dream, because in it I seek and obtain him who does not visit me in my wakefulness
modern: In dreams, I find pleasure because the dream brings me the lover who does not visit me when I am awake.

old: I saw him in my waking hours, and then it was pleasant; I see him just now in my dream, and it is (equally) pleasant
modern: Seeing the beloved in waking life was pleasant at that time, and seeing him in a dream is also pleasant right now.

old: Were there no such thing as wakefulness, my beloved (who visited me) in my dream would not depart from me
modern: If wakefulness did not exist to break the dream, the lover who visits me in my dreams would never leave.

old: The cruel one who would not favour me in my wakefulness, what right has he to torture me in my dreams?
modern: The cruel person who does not show kindness when awake torments me in my dreams. Why does this person who is unkind in person cause me pain in my dreams?

old: When I am asleep he rests on my shoulders, (but) when I awake he hastens into my soul
modern: When I am asleep, my lover rests on my shoulders, and when I wake up, he quickly enters my heart.

old: They who have no dear ones to behold in their dreams blame him who visits me not in my waking hours
modern: Women who do not see their lovers in dreams will blame their lovers for not visiting them in waking life.

old: The women of this place say he has forsaken me in my wakefulness I think they have not seen him visit me in my dreams
modern: The women of the town say my lover has left me in my waking life, but they do not see him in my dreams.

old: Live, O you evening are you (the former) evening? No, you are the season that slays (married) women
modern: Oh evening! You are not the evening of the past, but the time that devours the lives of women who have been with their lovers.

old: A long life to you, O dark evening! You are sightless Is your help-mate (also) as hard-hearted as mine
modern: O dim evening, hail! You have lost your light just like me. Is your mate also cruel-eyed like my spouse?

old: The evening that (once) came in with trembling and dimness (now) brings me an aversion for life and increasing sorrow
modern: The evening that once used to come trembling and pale now brings me an aversion to life and increasing sorrow.

old: In the absence of my lover, evening comes in like slayers on the field of slaughter
modern: When my lover is away, the evening comes like a merciless killer arriving at a slaughter.

old: What good have I done to morning (and) what evil to evening?.
modern: What good have I done to the morning, and what evil to the evening? The speaker laments that the morning used to bring relief from the pain of separation, but now it brings sorrow, and the evening used to bring joy in the beloved's presence, but now it brings grief.

old: Previous to my husband's departure, I know not the painful nature of evening
modern: I did not know that the evening could cause such suffering when my husband was with me and never left me alone. I only learned about the pain of the evening after he departed.

old: This malady buds forth in the morning, expands all day long and blossoms in the evening
modern: This disease of love buds in the morning, grows all day, and blooms in the evening.

old: The shepherd's flute now sounds as a fiery forerunner of night, and is become a weapon that slays (me)
modern: The shepherd's flute now acts as a messenger for the fiery evening that burns like a flame, and it sounds like a weapon that kills.

old: When night comes on confusing (everyone's) mind, the (whole) town will lose its sense and be plunged in sorrow
modern: When evening comes and confuses the mind, the whole town will be plunged into sorrow just as I am.

old: My (hitherto) unextinguished life is now lost in this bewildering night at the thought of him who has the nature of wealth
modern: My life, which had not died from the pain of separation, now dies in this bewitching evening as I think of my lover who has gone to seek wealth.

old: While we endure the unbearable sorrow, your eyes weep for him who is gone afar, and shun (the sight of) fragrant flowers
modern: Because she is crying for her lover who left, her eyes have lost their brightness and are now ashamed to look at the fragrant flowers.

old: The discoloured eyes that shed tears profusely seem to betray the unkindness of our beloved
modern: Tears rolling from discolored eyes seem to reveal to others that the person we love is not showing us any affection.

old: The shoulders that swelled on the day of our union (now) seem to announce our separation clearly (to the public)
modern: The shoulders that swelled with joy on the day of the wedding now look thin and announce the lover's departure.

old: In the absence of your consort, your shoulders having lost their former beauty and fulness, your bracelets of pure gold have become loose
modern: Because the lover left, the shoulders lost their former beauty and fullness and became thin, causing the green gold bracelets to slip off.

old: The (loosened) bracelets, and the shoulders from which the old beauty has faded, relate the cruelty of the pitiless one
modern: The speaker's wasted arms, once beautiful but now bare of bracelets, are telling everyone about the cruelty of a pitiless person.

old: I am greatly pained to hear you call him a cruel man, just because your shoulders are reduced and your bracelets loosened
modern: I am deeply hurt to hear people call my lover cruel just because my shoulders have grown thin and my armlets have slipped off.

old: Can you O my soul! gain glory by relating to the (so-called) cruel one the clamour of my fading shoulders?
modern: Will you gain any glory by going to tell my cruel lover about the pain of my withering shoulders and the noise they make?

old: When I once loosened the arms that were in embrace, the forehead of the gold-braceleted women turned sallow
modern: When I loosened my embracing arms, the forehead of the woman with the golden armlet turned pale.

old: When but a breath of breeze penetrated our embrace, her large cool eyes became sallow
modern: When a cool breeze entered our embrace, the woman's large, cool eyes lost their color.

old: Was it at the sight of what the bright forehead had done that the sallowness of her eyes became sad?
modern: The lover's eyes became pale and sad when she saw that her own forehead had turned pale from the cold breeze, realizing that her beauty was fading just like the complexion of her body.

old: O my soul, will you not think and tell me some medicine be it what it may, that can cure this incurable malady?
modern: My heart, can you not think of some medicine that can cure this incurable disease?

old: May you live, O my soul! While he is without love, for you to suffer is (simple) folly.
modern: My heart, live on! Since he does not love you, your longing for him is just foolishness.

old: O my soul! why remain (here) and suffer thinking (of him)? There are no lewd thoughts (of you) in him who has caused you this disease of sorrow
modern: O heart, why do you sit here and suffer thinking of him when he has no pity for you? Since he caused this sorrowful disease, he will not come to your rescue.

old: O my soul! take my eyes also with you, (if not), these would eat me up (in their desire) to see him
modern: O heart, take these eyes with you when you go to him, because they are so eager to see him that they will otherwise eat me up.

old: O my soul! can he who loves not though he is beloved, be forsaken saying he hates me (now)?
modern: Even though he does not love me back, can I really abandon him and think he hates me?

old: O my soul! when you see the dear one who remove dislike by intercourse, you are displeased and continue to be so Nay, your displeasure is (simply) false
modern: When you see your lover who removes your sulking by making love, you do not sulk, yet you now falsely burn with anger thinking they are cruel.

old: O my good soul, give up either lust or honour, as for me I can endure neither
modern: O good heart, you must give up either lust or shame, because I cannot endure both of them at the same time.

old: You are a fool, O my soul! to go after my departed one, while you mourn that he is not kind enough to favour you
modern: You are a fool, my heart, for chasing after the one who has left you, while you mourn that he does not show pity or love.

old: O my soul! to whom would you repair, while the dear one is within yourself?
modern: My heart, since your lover lives inside you, why do you go looking for him outside?

old: If I retain in my heart him who has left me without befriending me, I shall lose even the (inward) beauty that remains
modern: If I keep the person who left me in my heart, I will lose the inner beauty I still have.

old: The axe of lust can break the door of chastity which is bolted with the bolt of modesty
modern: Lust acts like an axe that breaks down the door of a woman's modesty, which is locked with the bolt of shame.

old: Even at midnight is my mind worried by lust, and this one thing, alas! is without mercy
modern: Lust is a merciless power that rules my mind even in the middle of the night.

old: I would conceal my lust, but alas, it yields not to my will but breaks out like a sneeze
modern: I try to hide my lust, but it bursts out like a sneeze without any warning.
